title: Data centres in India (2026): capacity, cities, companies, policy and power
description: India had about 1.6 to 1.8 GW of live data centre capacity in mid-2026, half of it in Mumbai. How many data centres there are, where, who runs them, the rules that apply and how they get power.
intro: India had between 1.6 GW and 1.8 GW of operational data centre capacity in mid-2026, depending on who counts and what they count; the government told Parliament in August 2026 that capacity had grown from 375 MW in 2020 to about 1,575 MW. Mumbai holds about half of it. Cushman & Wakefield counted 147 data centres across the top seven cities in H1 2026, with 509 MW under construction and 3,351 MW more planned. Forecasts for 2030 run from 4.5 GW to 8 GW. The constraint that decides which projects finish is increasingly power, not land or demand.
takeaways: Live capacity (mid-2026): about 1.6 GW (JLL), 1,789 MW (Cushman & Wakefield, top seven cities), 1,819 MW (Savills), with CBRE expecting 2 GW by the end of 2026.
Mumbai has about 50% of operational capacity; Chennai 12%, Delhi NCR 10%, Bengaluru 9%, Hyderabad 8%, Pune 7%, Kolkata 2%.

There is still no notified national data centre policy. Data centres of 5 MW IT load or more have infrastructure status (2022), and Budget 2026-27 added a tax holiday to 2047 for foreign cloud firms buying Indian data centre services.
The Central Electricity Authority estimates data centre power demand of about 17 GW by 2031-32.

sections.heading: How much data centre capacity does India have?

blocks.text: Five research houses published H1 2026 figures. They agree on the order of magnitude and disagree on the last few hundred MW because they count different things: some count only colocation, some add hyperscaler self-builds, some include enterprise and edge rooms, and most count only the top seven cities.

blocks.text: Additions in H1 2026 ranged from 85 MW (JLL) to 178 MW (Cushman & Wakefield) and 258 MW of IT load (Savills). Hyperscalers took more than 80% of absorption in the half, and pre-leased capacity roughly doubled to 1.15 GW.

sections.heading: How big will India’s data centre market be by 2030?

blocks.text: Crisil expects about three quarters of the roughly 6 GW now upcoming to sit in Visakhapatnam, Mumbai and Hyderabad, and the hyperscaler share of capacity to rise from 60 to 65% in FY26 to 75 to 80% by FY30, on contracts of 15 to 20 years.

sections.heading: Where are India’s data centres?

blocks.text: Mumbai leads because of its cable landing stations (13, with two more due in 2026), fibre density and the Thane-Belapur Road corridor, which alone holds about 675 MW. Hyderabad has the second-largest pipeline. Visakhapatnam has almost no live capacity but more than 4 GW announced, led by Google’s AI hub; Jamnagar in Gujarat is the other gigawatt-scale site, built around Reliance’s solar capacity.

sections.heading: What policy applies to data centres in India?

blocks.text: There is no notified national data centre policy. MeitY published a draft in November 2020 that never came into force, and reopened consultations in August 2025. In October 2026 NITI Aayog issued a non-binding evaluation framework that asks each state for a data centre approval matrix and a single clearance portal.

items: Infrastructure status: data centres of at least 5 MW IT load were added to the Harmonised Master List under Communication on 11 October 2022, which eases institutional credit.

Tax: Budget 2026-27 exempts foreign cloud companies from tax to tax year 2046-47 on income from serving global customers using Indian data centre services; a 15% cost safe harbour applies where the Indian provider is related.
States: 11 states have data centre policies with capital, power tariff, stamp duty and electricity duty incentives. Several have lapsed or been replaced in 2026.

blocks.text: Demand is also driven by data rules: RBI requires payment system data to be stored only in India (2018); SEBI requires regulated entities’ cloud data to stay within India (2023); CERT-In requires 180 days of logs kept in India and five years of subscriber records from data centres (2022); and the DPDP Rules 2025, with most duties from May 2027, let the government require significant data fiduciaries to keep specified data in India.

sections.heading: How do India’s data centres get power?

blocks.text: Data centre load is still less than 1% of India’s installed power capacity, but the Central Electricity Authority puts demand at about 17 GW by 2031-32. Locally the numbers are already large: Crisil estimates that by FY2030 data centre capacity could equal about 60% of Mumbai’s current peak demand and about 80% of Visakhapatnam’s.

Structure Research reports that the roughly 6 GW of grid capacity MSEDCL allocated to Navi Mumbai data centres is close to fully committed, pushing new builds to Panvel, Taloja and Rasayani where new substations can be built. For a site buyer, the document behind the MW and the date of the connection matter more than distance to a line.

sections.heading: What does a data centre cost in India?

blocks.text: Cushman & Wakefield benchmarks construction at US$7.4 million per MW, about 23% below Malaysia, and US$9.0 million per MW for AI capacity. SBI, citing JM Financial, gives ₹50 to 55 crore per MW for an air-cooled Tier III build and up to ₹75 crore for AI or Tier IV.

Wholesale colocation for 5 MW and above was quoted at ₹6,000 to 7,500 per kW per month in Mumbai in H1 2025, the latest published table. Anarock puts land for 100 to 500 MW parks at ₹3 to 10 crore per acre and for small suburban Mumbai sites at ₹35 to 60 crore.

sections.heading: AI data centres and GPUs in India

blocks.text: The IndiaAI Mission made about 38,000 GPUs available to researchers and startups at around ₹65 per GPU-hour by February 2026. The gigawatt campuses announced since 2025 (Google in Visakhapatnam, Reliance in Jamnagar, Tata’s HyperVault with OpenAI as first customer) are AI-driven, with rack densities of 30 to 60 kW against 8 to 10 kW in conventional halls.

faqs.question: How many data centres are there in India?
faqs.answer: Cushman & Wakefield counted 147 operational data centres run by 33 operators across the top seven cities in H1 2026; Anarock counted 164. Counts differ because some trackers include enterprise and edge rooms. By capacity, India had about 1.6 to 1.8 GW live in mid-2026.

faqs.question: What is the total data centre capacity in India in 2026?
faqs.answer: About 1,575 MW according to the government (August 2026), 1,789 MW across the top seven cities according to Cushman & Wakefield (H1 2026) and 1,819 MW of IT load according to Savills. CBRE expects 2 GW by the end of 2026.

faqs.question: Which city has the most data centres in India?
faqs.answer: Mumbai, with 890 MW or about half of India’s operational capacity in H1 2026, most of it in Navi Mumbai along Thane-Belapur Road. Chennai is second with 214 MW.

faqs.question: Which state has the most data centres in India?
faqs.answer: Maharashtra, through Mumbai, Navi Mumbai and Pune, holds well over half of operational capacity. Tamil Nadu (Chennai) is next. For announced pipeline, Andhra Pradesh (Visakhapatnam) and Telangana (Hyderabad) are growing fastest.

faqs.question: Does India have a national data centre policy?
faqs.answer: Not a notified one. MeitY’s 2020 draft never came into force and consultations reopened in August 2025. National measures in force are infrastructure status for data centres of 5 MW or more (2022) and the Budget 2026-27 tax holiday for foreign cloud firms using Indian data centres.

faqs.question: How much electricity will Indian data centres need?
faqs.answer: The Central Electricity Authority estimates about 17 GW of data centre demand by 2031-32, against less than 1% of installed capacity today.

faqs.question: How much does it cost to build a data center in India per MW?
faqs.answer: About US$7.4 million per MW on Cushman & Wakefield’s benchmark, or ₹50 to 55 crore per MW for air-cooled Tier III and up to ₹75 crore for AI or Tier IV builds (JM Financial via SBI), excluding land.

faqs.question: What are the largest data centre projects in India?
faqs.answer: Announced gigawatt-scale campuses include Google’s AI hub in Visakhapatnam (about 1 GW, about US$15 billion) and Reliance’s AI build in Jamnagar. Most are in early stages; Cushman & Wakefield counts more than 4 GW announced in Visakhapatnam alone.

title: How to find a data centre site in India (2026): power first, then fibre, land, water and risk
description: Pick an Indian data centre site in this order: written power evidence, fibre and cable landings, land and zoning, water, physical risk, then state policy. City by city comparison with sources.
intro: The best location for a data centre in India is the one that can show a dated power connection for the full load, not the one nearest a substation. Mumbai has half of India’s operational capacity because of its 13 cable landing stations, but the roughly 6 GW of grid capacity allocated to Navi Mumbai data centres is close to fully committed. Chennai and Hyderabad have spare colocation (vacancy of 26.7% and 28.0% in H1 2026), and Visakhapatnam has more than 4 GW announced. Screen power evidence first, then fibre, land and zoning, water, seismic and flood risk, and the state policy that applies.
takeaways: Rank sites by the document behind the MW (connection offer, sanctioned load, signed agreement), not by distance to a line.
Mumbai and Chennai have the cable landings; Hyderabad, Noida and Pune are inland markets that depend on terrestrial fibre.
Seismic zones in the IS 1893 (Part 1) town list (2002 edition, zones retained in 2016): Delhi IV; Mumbai, Chennai, Pune, Kolkata and Ahmedabad III; Bengaluru, Hyderabad and Visakhapatnam II.
Several state policies lapsed or were replaced in 2026, so check which incentives are actually open on the date you apply.

blocks.text: Each check can kill a site, so run the cheapest decisive check first. In India that is power: a large load needs a dedicated connection from the discom or the state transmission utility, and the date on that connection usually sets the project schedule. NITI Aayog’s October 2026 framework now asks states to verify power and water capacity before clearing data centre projects.

sections.heading: Power: the check that decides the schedule

blocks.text: Structure Research reports that MSEDCL allocated about 6 GW of grid capacity to Navi Mumbai data centres and that committed and under-construction capacity is approaching it, which is pushing new builds to Panvel, Taloja and Rasayani where new substations can be built. Crisil estimates that by FY2030 data centre capacity could equal about 60% of Mumbai’s current peak demand and about 80% of Visakhapatnam’s.

Some state policies write the connection terms down: Tamil Nadu’s 2021 policy offered dual grid supply for loads of 50 MW and above and an extra feeder above 100 MW, and West Bengal’s 2021 policy offered dual grid supply. Treat these as eligibility for a connection, not as capacity on a given date.

sections.heading: Fibre and cable landings

blocks.text: About 95% of India’s international bandwidth is handled in the Mumbai region. Mumbai has 13 cable landing stations and Chennai 7, with more under construction in both. Visakhapatnam is being built as an east coast gateway: Google’s America-India Connect, announced in February 2026, includes routes from Visakhapatnam to South Africa and to Malaysia.

For an AI training campus, latency to a landing station matters less than power and land; for interconnection and cloud regions it matters more. Decide which you are building before weighting this step.

sections.heading: Land, water and physical risk

blocks.text: Anarock prices land for 100 to 500 MW parks at ₹3 to 10 crore per acre and for small suburban Mumbai sites at ₹35 to 60 crore, and advises buying 30 to 50% more land than phase 1 needs. Groundwater cannot be assumed: under the CGWA guidelines of September 2020, new industries other than MSMEs get no groundwater permit in over-exploited assessment units, and SBI names Bengaluru, Chennai and Gurugram as water-stressed data centre metros.

Physical risk is mostly known in advance: Mumbai recorded 944 mm of rain in 24 hours on 26 July 2005, Chennai’s Meenambakkam station recorded 1,178.3 mm in November 2015, and Cyclone Hudhud crossed the coast over Visakhapatnam in October 2014. Airport height limits apply within 20 km of visual and 56 km of instrument approach airports, and both Navi Mumbai and Noida now have new airports close to data centre clusters.

faqs.question: What is the best location for a data centre in India?
faqs.answer: It depends on what you are building. Mumbai has the cable landings and half of operational capacity but a tight grid in Navi Mumbai; Chennai has landings and spare capacity; Hyderabad has the second-largest pipeline and seismic zone II; Visakhapatnam has more than 4 GW announced. The deciding factor is a dated power connection for the full load.

faqs.question: How do I choose a site for a data center in India?
faqs.answer: Screen in this order: written power evidence, fibre and cable landings, land title and zoning, water, seismic, flood and airport height limits, then the state policy that applies on the date you apply.

faqs.question: Which Indian cities have cable landing stations for data centres?
faqs.answer: Mumbai (13 stations, two more due in 2026) and Chennai (7, two under construction) are the main ones. Visakhapatnam is being developed as an east coast gateway, and a station at Tajpur near Kolkata is under construction.

faqs.question: Is Navi Mumbai running out of power for data centres?
faqs.answer: Structure Research reports that the roughly 6 GW of grid capacity MSEDCL allocated to Navi Mumbai data centres is close to fully committed, and that new builds are moving to Panvel, Taloja and Rasayani where new substations can be built.

faqs.question: Which seismic zone are India’s data centre cities in?
faqs.answer: Under IS 1893 (Part 1): Delhi is zone IV; Mumbai, Thane, Chennai, Pune, Kolkata and Ahmedabad are zone III; Bengaluru, Hyderabad and Visakhapatnam are zone II.

title: Approvals needed for a data centre in India (2026): permits, NOCs and who issues them
description: A data centre in India needs land and building approvals, environmental clearance above 20,000 sq m, pollution board consents, groundwater, airport height and fire NOCs, a diesel licence and electrical inspection.
intro: There is no single data centre licence in India. A project collects approvals from several authorities: land allotment and building plan approval from the state or local authority, environmental clearance under the EIA Notification 2006 if the built-up area is 20,000 sq m or more, Consent to Establish and Consent to Operate from the state pollution control board, a groundwater NOC, an airport height clearance, a fire NOC, a licence to store diesel and an electrical inspector’s approval before energisation. NITI Aayog’s October 2026 framework asks every state to publish a data centre approval matrix and run a single clearance portal because these sit with so many offices.
takeaways: Environmental clearance: the government told the Rajya Sabha in August 2026, as quoted by Countercurrents, that data centres do not need it as such, only as building projects of 20,000 sq m or more (item 8(a)) or townships (item 8(b)).
Pollution board category: CPCB’s January 2025 classification puts data centres by their gensets: 1 MVA or more on liquid fuel is Orange, on gas Green, under 1,000 kVA needs no added category.
Diesel: if it is Class B fuel (usual; confirm with PESO), below 2,500 litres needs no licence, 2,500 to 25,000 litres is licensed by the district authority and more needs a PESO licence.
Fire: the National Building Code 2016 classes data centres as occupancy E-3 and requires automatic fire detection.

sections.heading: Does a data centre need environmental clearance in India?

blocks.text: Item 8(a) of the EIA Notification 2006 covers building and construction projects of 20,000 sq m or more and below 1,50,000 sq m of built-up area; item 8(b) covers townships and area development projects of 50 ha or more or 1,50,000 sq m or more. In a Rajya Sabha reply on 6 August 2026, as quoted by Countercurrents, the government said data centres do not per se require clearance but do when they fall under 8(a) or 8(b).

Large campuses commonly exceed 20,000 sq m of built-up area. SEIAA Maharashtra granted clearance on 21 November 2025 for Nxtra’s expansion at Mahape, Navi Mumbai: two data centre buildings, two DG buildings and a substation, 76,930 sq m built-up in total. STT GDC’s Mumbai campus was cleared the same way. There is no data centre exemption: in August 2025 the Supreme Court quashed the January 2025 note that had exempted industrial sheds from 8(a).

sections.heading: What are CTE and CTO, and which category is a data centre?

blocks.text: Consent to Establish (CTE) is the state pollution control board’s permission to build; Consent to Operate (CTO) is its permission to run. Both are issued under the Water Act 1974 and the Air Act 1981, and the conditions follow the sector’s category.

rows: Data centres whose only pollution source is gensets, total under 1,000 kVA
Gensets totalling 1 MVA or more on liquid fuel
Gensets totalling 1 MVA or more on cleaner or gaseous fuel
Building construction, built-up area of 20,000 sq m or more

blocks.text: A campus with diesel gensets above 1 MVA is therefore Orange, for which boards may grant CTO for up to 10 years, against 15 years for Green. State boards can keep their own lists, and none was found that names data centres, so confirm the category with the state board for the specific site.

sections.heading: Diesel storage and genset rules

blocks.text: The Petroleum Rules 2002 split fuels by flash point: Class B is 23°C to below 65°C. PESO lists diesel (HSD) among products that need a licence. Class B storage below 2,500 litres needs no licence, the district authority licenses 2,500 to 25,000 litres, and larger quantities need a PESO licence, applied for through the National Single Window System. Confirm the class of the fuel you store with PESO; at data centre volumes it decides which licence you need.

Genset emission limits for engines up to 800 kW (CPCB IV+) were notified by G.S.R. 804(E), as cited by CAQM, and apply from 1 July 2023. The 2 to 3 MW sets typical in data centres are above 800 kW and remain under the older concentration standards.

items.label: Diesel generators and backup power rules

sections.heading: Fire NOC and electrical inspection

blocks.text: The National Building Code 2016, Part 4, puts electronic data processing centres and computer installations in occupancy E-3. For E-3 it requires an automatic fire detection and alarm system, allows clean agents, water mist or hypoxic air for protection, and allows CO2 or inert gas flooding for electrical panels. The fire NOC itself is issued by the state fire service under state law.

Under the CEA safety regulations of 2023, each state notifies the voltage up to which owners may self-certify. Andhra Pradesh’s order of 11 March 2026 sets 33 kV: installations above it are inspected by the electrical inspector, and generating units above 10 kW are inspected before commissioning. A campus with a 66, 110 or 220 kV substation and diesel gensets therefore needs the inspector before energisation.

sections.heading: Obligations that start once the data centre runs

items: CERT-In directions of 28 April 2022: report listed cyber incidents within 6 hours, keep ICT logs for 180 days in India, and keep validated subscriber records for 5 years.
Battery Waste Management Rules 2022: producers carry extended producer responsibility under the CPCB EPR system; confirm how waste UPS batteries must be handed over.
Energy codes: BEE’s ECBC 2017 and ECSBC 2024 include provisions relevant to data centres and apply where the state has adopted them.
Refrigerants: India’s HFC freeze starts on 1 January 2028, with an 85% cut by 2047, which affects chiller refrigerant choice.

faqs.question: What approvals are needed to set up a data centre in India?
faqs.answer: Typically: land allotment or purchase and any change of land use, building plan approval, environmental clearance if built-up area is 20,000 sq m or more, Consent to Establish and Consent to Operate from the state pollution control board, a groundwater NOC, an AAI height clearance near airports, a diesel storage licence, a fire NOC and electrical inspection before energisation.

faqs.question: Is there a data center licence in India?
faqs.answer: No single licence. A data centre collects approvals from several authorities. NITI Aayog’s October 2026 framework asks each state to publish a data centre approval matrix and run a single clearance portal.

faqs.question: Does a data centre need environmental clearance?
faqs.answer: Not as a category. It needs clearance as a building project when built-up area is 20,000 sq m or more (item 8(a) of the EIA Notification 2006) or as a township of 50 ha or 1,50,000 sq m or more (item 8(b)), according to the government’s Rajya Sabha reply of 6 August 2026 as quoted.

faqs.question: What is CTE and CTO for a data centre?
faqs.answer: Consent to Establish and Consent to Operate are the state pollution control board’s permissions to build and to run, under the Water Act 1974 and the Air Act 1981. For a data centre the category follows the gensets: 1 MVA or more on diesel is Orange under CPCB’s January 2025 classification.

faqs.question: Which pollution category is a data centre in India?
faqs.answer: CPCB’s January 2025 classification says data centres whose only pollution source is gensets are classified by genset capacity and fuel: Orange for 1 MVA or more on liquid fuel, Green on gaseous fuel, no added category below 1,000 kVA. A built-up area of 20,000 sq m or more is separately Orange.

faqs.question: Do I need a licence to store diesel at a data centre?
faqs.answer: Under the Petroleum Rules 2002, Class B fuel below 2,500 litres needs no licence, 2,500 to 25,000 litres needs a district licence and more needs a PESO licence. PESO lists diesel (HSD) as a product requiring a licence; confirm its class for your fuel with PESO.

faqs.question: Do data centres need a fire NOC?
faqs.answer: Yes. The state fire service issues it under state law, and the National Building Code 2016 classes data centres as occupancy E-3, which requires automatic fire detection and alarm.

title: How to set up a data centre in India (2026): the sequence from entity to energisation
description: Setting up a data centre in India runs in nine steps: size the load, form the entity, pick a state, confirm power, secure land, design to Indian codes, get approvals, inspect and energise.
intro: To set up a data centre in India, fix the load and tier, form an Indian company (Khaitan & Co reads the FDI policy as allowing 100% foreign investment under the automatic route for a company doing only data centre business), choose a state whose policy is actually open, and confirm a dated power connection before you buy land. Then secure the land, design to the National Building Code and IS 1893, collect the pre-construction approvals, build, pass fire and electrical inspection, and take Consent to Operate. Data centres of 5 MW IT load or more have infrastructure status, which helps on debt. The order matters more than any single permit: a site without a dated power connection is not a site.
takeaways: Power before land: get the voltage, MW and date in writing for each candidate site.
Foreign investors: 100% under the automatic route according to Khaitan & Co’s reading of the FDI policy, except investors from land-border countries, who need approval under Press Note 3.
Data centres of 5 MW IT load or more are infrastructure (Harmonised Master List, 11 October 2022).
The detailed permit list, with authorities and thresholds, is on the approvals page.

sections.heading: The nine steps

rows: 1. Size the load and the tier
Fix the IT load in MW, the phasing, the target tier and the rack density. AI halls run 30 to 60 kW per rack against 8 to 10 kW in conventional ones, which changes power, cooling and land.

Khaitan & Co reads the FDI policy as allowing 100% foreign investment under the automatic route for a company doing only data centre business (data centres are not a named sector). Investors from countries that share a land border with India need government approval under Press Note 3 (2020).
3. Shortlist states and check which policies are open
Compare the state policies that are in force on the date you will apply. Tamil Nadu’s 2021 policy covered projects up to 31 March 2026; Uttar Pradesh replaced its 2021 policy in July 2026.
4. Confirm the power path before buying land

Get the serving discom or transmission utility, the voltage, the MW and the date in writing for each candidate site. In Navi Mumbai the grid capacity allocated to data centres is reported close to fully committed.
5. Secure land and run site due diligence
Take an allotment from a state development authority or buy private land, then check title, land use, flood and seismic exposure, groundwater status and airport height limits.

National Building Code 2016 Part 4 (occupancy E-3), IS 1893 (Part 1):2016 for seismic design, the state’s adopted energy code, and the BIS adoptions of ISO/IEC 22237 and 30134 where you want a recognised standard.
Building plan, environmental clearance if built-up area is 20,000 sq m or more, Consent to Establish, groundwater NOC, airport height clearance and the diesel storage licence.
8. Build, inspect and get the operating consents
Fire NOC, electrical inspector approval before energisation and Consent to Operate from the state pollution control board.
9. Energise, claim incentives and start operating compliance
Register for state incentives through the single window, and set up CERT-In reporting and log retention, battery and e-waste handling, and energy and water reporting.

items.label: Approvals for a data centre in India

sections.heading: Entity, foreign investment and finance

blocks.text: Khaitan & Co notes that 100% FDI is allowed under the automatic route for Indian companies engaged only in the data centre business; if the company also owns fibre or other telecom assets, the conditions for those sectors apply, and investors from countries sharing a land border with India need government approval under Press Note 3 (2020).

Data centres housed in a dedicated building with at least 5 MW of IT load were added to the Harmonised Master List of Infrastructure on 11 October 2022. Anarock reports long-tenor debt for data centres at about 9.5 to 10.5% for up to 12 years, helped by that status.

sections.heading: Choosing the state

blocks.text: State policies decide capital subsidy, stamp duty, electricity duty and power terms. Several changed in 2026: Uttar Pradesh notified a new policy on 9 July 2026 that repeals the 2021 one, and Tamil Nadu’s 2021 policy applied to data centres set up from 1 April 2021 to 31 March 2026. Read the notified text and its validity date, not a summary.

items.label: Infrastructure status, tax holiday and DC SEZs

sections.heading: Power and land, in that order

blocks.text: A large data centre needs a dedicated connection from the discom or the state transmission utility. Structure Research reports that the roughly 6 GW of grid capacity MSEDCL allocated to Navi Mumbai data centres is close to fully committed, which is why new campuses there are moving to sites where new substations can be built. NITI Aayog has asked states to verify power and water capacity before clearing projects.

Allotment from a state development authority usually comes with defined use and building norms. Uttar Pradesh’s 2026 policy, for example, gives data centres FAR 3.0 free plus 1.0 chargeable, 60% ground coverage and a 100% stamp duty exemption on land bought or leased from a government authority.

sections.heading: Design standards to plan around

blocks.text: The National Building Code 2016 classes data centres as occupancy E-3. Seismic design follows IS 1893 (Part 1):2016; the 2025 revision that added a Zone VI was reported withdrawn in March 2026. BIS has adopted the ISO/IEC 22237 facility series and the ISO/IEC 30134 metrics (PUE, WUE, CUE); they are voluntary unless made mandatory by a quality control order.
Uttar Pradesh reimburses 25% of Tier III and 50% of Tier IV certification charges by Uptime, TIA or an equivalent agency, one of the few places a certification cost is offset.

sections.heading: After energisation

blocks.text: Operating obligations start on day one: CERT-In’s 2022 directions require incident reports within 6 hours, 180 days of logs kept in India and 5 years of subscriber records from data centres; and producers carry extended producer responsibility for UPS batteries under the Battery Waste Management Rules 2022, so confirm the hand-over route for waste batteries.

sections.heading: How Invariant helps

blocks.text: Invariant works on the steps that decide whether a site is real: it checks how the site gets power and the evidence behind the MW, screens seismic, flood, groundwater and airport height risk, and maps the central and state approvals with the authority behind each one. Send the state, the MW and the date you need power.

faqs.question: How do I set up a data centre in India?
faqs.answer: Size the load and tier, form an Indian company, choose a state whose policy is open, confirm a dated power connection, secure and diligence the land, design to the National Building Code and IS 1893, get the pre-construction approvals, pass fire and electrical inspection, then take Consent to Operate and energise.

faqs.question: Can a foreign company set up a data centre in India?
faqs.answer: Yes. Khaitan & Co reads the FDI policy as allowing 100% FDI under the automatic route for an Indian company engaged only in data centre business; data centres are not a named sector. Investors from countries sharing a land border with India need government approval under Press Note 3 (2020).

faqs.question: How do I start a data center business in India?
faqs.answer: Most new entrants either build and lease capacity (colocation or build-to-suit for hyperscalers) or buy capacity from an operator. Either way the first questions are power, land and the state policy; the approvals list follows from the site and the size.

faqs.question: Do data centres get infrastructure status in India?
faqs.answer: Yes, data centres in a dedicated building with at least 5 MW of IT load were added to the Harmonised Master List of Infrastructure on 11 October 2022, which eases access to long-term credit.

faqs.question: What standards should an Indian data centre be designed to?
faqs.answer: The National Building Code 2016 (occupancy E-3), IS 1893 (Part 1):2016 for seismic design, the energy code your state has adopted, and voluntarily the BIS adoptions of ISO/IEC 22237 and ISO/IEC 30134.

title: Data centre cost per MW in India (2026): ₹35 to 75 crore to build, plus land
description: Building a data centre in India costs about US$7.4 million per MW (Cushman & Wakefield) or ₹35 to 75 crore per MW depending on scale, tier and cooling. Benchmarks, land, rents and financing.
intro: A data centre in India costs roughly ₹35 crore to ₹75 crore per MW of IT load to build, before land, depending on scale, tier and cooling. Cushman & Wakefield benchmarks US$7.4 million per MW, about 23% below Malaysia and 26% below Australia, and US$9.0 million per MW for AI capacity. JM Financial, cited by SBI, puts an air-cooled Tier III build at ₹50 to 55 crore per MW and AI or Tier IV at up to ₹75 crore. Land adds ₹3 crore to ₹60 crore per acre depending on size and city, and long-tenor debt costs about 9.5 to 10.5%.
takeaways: Cushman & Wakefield: US$7.4 million per MW; US$9.0 million per MW for AI capacity.
JM Financial via SBI: ₹50 to 55 crore per MW for air-cooled Tier III, up to ₹75 crore for AI or Tier IV, ₹35 to 45 crore at large scale.
Anarock: ₹40 to 45 crore per MW (low) to ₹65 to 70 crore per MW (high) for a greenfield Tier III N+1 build.
Wholesale colocation for 5 MW and above rented at about ₹6,000 to 7,500 per kW per month in H1 2025.

sections.heading: How much does it cost to build a data centre in India per MW?

rows: US$7.4 million per MW; US$9.0 million per MW for AI capacity
₹40 to 45 crore per MW to ₹65 to 70 crore per MW (US$4.8 to 8.4 million)

blocks.text: None of these benchmarks says it includes land, and Anarock prices land separately. Crisil puts Indian development costs about one fifth below several Asia Pacific peers.

A cross-check from the sector level: ICRA expected third-party capacity to grow from 1,250 MW in FY2025 to 2,400 to 2,500 MW by FY2028 with about ₹90,000 crore of capex, which works out (our calculation) to roughly ₹72 to 78 crore per MW added.

sections.heading: What moves the number

items: Cooling and density: Anarock maps in-row cooling to 3 to 10 kW per rack (the most common in India), rear-door to 10 to 20 kW and direct liquid cooling to 40 to 100 kW or more; AI racks run 30 to 60 kW.
Tier: the jump from Tier III to Tier IV is the difference between the ₹50 to 55 crore and the ₹75 crore bands above.
Efficiency targets: SBI reports leading Indian operators at PUE 1.4 to 1.5 and MeitY AI cloud tenders asking for below 1.35, which pushes design toward more efficient cooling.
Grid connection: who pays for the dedicated line, bay and substation is set by the discom or transmission utility for each site, and can be a large line item on a greenfield campus.

sections.heading: Land cost

rows: ₹35 to 60 crore (Mumbai suburbs); ₹4 to 10 crore (secondary cities)

blocks.text: Recent transactions sit inside these bands: Amazon Data Services bought 10.6 acres from Lodha for ₹125.13 crore in June 2026, about ₹11.8 crore per acre (our calculation).

sections.heading: What does colocation rent for in India?

blocks.text: Cushman & Wakefield’s H1 2025 report is the latest with a published rent table, in ₹ per kW per month for standard 5 to 7 kVA racks.
Crisil says Indian rents are 30 to 35% below peer markets and that contract tenors are now 15 to 20 years.

sections.heading: Financing and incentives

blocks.text: Infrastructure status for data centres of at least 5 MW IT load (11 October 2022) eases access to long-term credit; Anarock reports debt at about 9.5 to 10.5% for up to 12 years. State policies cut the effective cost further through capital subsidy, stamp duty exemption and electricity duty exemption: Uttar Pradesh’s 2026 policy, for example, exempts 100% of stamp duty on government land and gives a 25% land subsidy in the Noida region.

title: Data centre site due diligence in India (2026): the feasibility checklist
description: Due diligence on an Indian data centre site checks title and land use, power evidence, seismic zone, flood and cyclone history, groundwater status, airport height limits and the approvals path.
intro: Due diligence on a data centre site in India answers one question first: can this parcel get the full load, at the voltage needed, on a date you can underwrite? After power come title and land use, groundwater (no new industry other than MSMEs gets a groundwater permit in an over-exploited unit under the 2020 CGWA guidelines), seismic zone under IS 1893, flood and cyclone history from IMD records, airport height limits within 20 or 56 km of an airport, and the approvals the project will need. NITI Aayog’s October 2026 framework now asks states to verify power and water capacity before clearing data centre projects, so the same questions will come from the state.
takeaways: Power evidence is graded by the document: a written connection offer or sanctioned load beats proximity to a substation.
Groundwater: check the assessment unit on CGWB’s INGRES; 730 of 6,762 units (10.8%) were over-exploited in the 2025 assessment.
Seismic: design to IS 1893 (Part 1):2016; the 2025 map with a Zone VI was reported withdrawn in March 2026.
Airports: height clearance is needed within 20 km of visual and 56 km of instrument approach airports; it is valid 8 years and free.

sections.heading: Power evidence: the first and most decisive check

blocks.text: The test is the document behind the MW. A parcel near a 220 kV substation is not a 100 MW site until the utility has said, in writing, how much it can supply and when, and what upgrades that depends on. Crisil estimates that by FY2030 data centre capacity could equal about 60% of Mumbai’s current peak demand and about 80% of Visakhapatnam’s, so headroom near today’s clusters is being used quickly.

items.label: Grid connection: DISCOM, STU and CTU paths
Power studies for Indian data centre sites

sections.heading: Water and groundwater

blocks.text: Under the CGWA guidelines of 24 September 2020, any new or expanding industry or infrastructure project that abstracts groundwater needs a NOC unless exempt, and no new industry other than MSMEs gets one in an over-exploited unit. Infrastructure projects are treated as location specific and are not barred outright. Whether a data centre is treated as industry or infrastructure is not settled in the guidelines’ text, so confirm it with the authority for the specific site.

The 2025 national assessment classed 730 of 6,762 units (10.8%) as over-exploited, concentrated in the north-west, west and south. CGWB-based reporting says every assessment unit in Bengaluru Urban is over-exploited.

sections.heading: Seismic, flood, cyclone and coast

blocks.text: IS 1893 (Part 1) puts Delhi in zone IV, Mumbai, Chennai, Pune, Kolkata and Ahmedabad in zone III, and Bengaluru, Hyderabad and Visakhapatnam in zone II. Flood records to check against include 944 mm in 24 hours at Mumbai’s Santacruz on 26 July 2005 and 1,178.3 mm in November 2015 at Chennai’s Meenambakkam. Cyclone Hudhud crossed the coast over Visakhapatnam on 12 October 2014 with winds of about 180 km/h and a 1.4 m storm surge.
Near the coast, the CRZ Notification 2019 sets No Development Zones of 50 m from the high tide line in densely populated rural areas (CRZ-IIIA) and 200 m elsewhere in CRZ-III.

sections.heading: Airport height limits

blocks.text: Under G.S.R. 751(E) of 2015, a height clearance from AAI is needed within 20 km of a visual approach airport and 56 km of an instrument approach airport. It is valid for 8 years and has no fee. Navi Mumbai International Airport began commercial flights on 25 December 2025 and Noida International Airport on 15 June 2026; AAI advised in July 2025 that no construction should take place within 20 km of the Noida airport without height clearance.

sections.heading: How Invariant helps

blocks.text: Invariant runs this checklist on Indian sites: it checks how the site gets power and the evidence behind the MW, screens seismic zone, flood and cyclone history, groundwater status and airport height limits, and maps the central and state approvals with the authority behind each. Send the coordinates or the state, the MW and the date you need power.

faqs.question: What is data centre site due diligence?
faqs.answer: A structured check of whether a parcel can become a data centre on your timeline: power evidence, title and land use, water, seismic, flood and cyclone risk, airport height limits and the approvals path.

faqs.question: What should a data centre site selection checklist in India include?
faqs.answer: Power (utility, voltage, MW, date, in writing), title and encumbrances, land use and FAR, groundwater unit status, seismic zone, flood and cyclone records, coastal zone limits, airport height clearance, environmental clearance threshold and state policy eligibility.

faqs.question: How do I check if groundwater can be used at a site in India?
faqs.answer: Find the site’s assessment unit on CGWB’s INGRES system. In over-exploited units the 2020 CGWA guidelines bar new industries other than MSMEs from getting a groundwater NOC; infrastructure projects are assessed case by case.

faqs.question: Do I need AAI height clearance for a data centre?
faqs.answer: Yes, if the site is within 20 km of a visual approach airport or 56 km of an instrument approach airport, unless a colour coded zoning map shows the building is below the permissible height. Clearance is valid for 8 years and has no fee.

faqs.question: What is a data center feasibility study in India?
faqs.answer: A first pass over the same checklist, run before land is bought: whether power can be had at the needed MW and date, whether the land and water work, and which physical risks and approvals apply. It ends in a go, no-go or conditional go.

title: Data centre land in India (2026): acres per MW, land prices, parks and powered land
description: Data centre land in India runs ₹3 to 60 crore per acre and about half an acre per MW on Anarock’s bands. Prices, recent deals, data centre parks, FAR rules and what makes land powered.
intro: Data centre land in India costs from about ₹3 crore per acre for 100 to 500 MW parks to ₹35 to 60 crore per acre for small sites in Mumbai’s suburbs, on Anarock’s 2026 benchmarks. Its size bands imply roughly half an acre per MW of IT load. Savills counted more than 120 acres of data centre land transacted in H1 2026. Land becomes powered land only when the utility has committed MW and a date in writing; in India most large sites are allotted by state development authorities, several of which now run dedicated data centre parks.
takeaways: Anarock size bands: 5 to 10 MW on 2 to 5 acres, up to 100 to 500 MW on 50 to 200 acres (midpoints about 0.4 to 0.5 acre per MW, our calculation).
Recent deals: STT GDC paid ₹282 crore for 3.48 acres with a building in Navi Mumbai; Amazon Data Services paid ₹125.13 crore for 10.6 acres from Lodha.
Parks: YEIDA’s 100-acre Data Centre Park in Sector 28; Maharashtra’s green data centre parks; Karnataka’s planned 500 MW park near Hoskote.
Building norms help: Uttar Pradesh (2026) and West Bengal (2021) allow FAR 3.0 plus 1.0 purchasable for data centres.

sections.heading: How much land does a data centre need in India?

columns: Acres per MW at the midpoint (our calculation)

blocks.text: No Indian authority publishes a standard. The ratio depends on how many storeys the building has, the FAR the state allows, and how much of the site goes to the substation, generators and fuel. Anarock advises buying 30 to 50% more land than phase 1 needs.

sections.heading: Data centre land prices in India

rows: ₹35 to 60 crore in Mumbai suburbs; ₹4 to 10 crore in secondary cities
100 to 500 MW (Navi Mumbai, outer Chennai, Noida parks)
3.48 acres with a building, TTC Industrial Area, Navi Mumbai

blocks.text: Savills counted more than 120 acres of data centre land transacted in H1 2026.

sections.heading: Data centre parks in India

items: Uttar Pradesh: YEIDA lists a 100-acre Data Centre Park in Sector 28, applied for through Nivesh Mitra. UP’s 2026 policy defines a park as at least 40 MW of load.
Maharashtra: the IT/ITeS Policy 2023 says MIDC will take up data centre parks with prior clearances for land allotted to data centres.
Karnataka: a 500 MW data centre park near Hoskote by 2031, with solar power and treated water committed, and 500 MW at Mysuru and Mangaluru.
Andhra Pradesh: Google’s subsidiary was reported to receive about 480 acres across three locations in the Visakhapatnam region at a 25% discount to market price as part of its incentive package.
Private parks: Lodha has earmarked about 400 acres at Palava for data centres, as reported by Business Standard in April 2026.

sections.heading: FAR, ground coverage and stamp duty

blocks.text: Uttar Pradesh’s 2026 policy gives data centres base FAR 3.0 free plus 1.0 chargeable, keeps basement parking, storage and DG space out of FAR, extends service FAR to 40% for DG sets, allows 60% ground coverage and unrestricted floor-to-ceiling height subject to overall height rules. It exempts 100% of stamp duty on land bought or leased from a government authority and gives a land subsidy of 25% of sector rates in the Noida and YEIDA region and 50% in Bundelkhand and Purvanchal.
West Bengal’s 2021 policy also allows FAR 3.0 plus 1.0 purchasable and 60% ground coverage.

sections.heading: Powered land in India

blocks.text: Powered land means land with deliverable electricity for the load, documented by the utility, not land near a substation. India has no public listing market for it the way the US does; most large campuses are assembled through state allotments and private purchases and then connected through the discom or the state transmission utility. In Navi Mumbai, where Structure Research reports the data centre grid allocation is close to fully committed, a site with a connection already in place is worth much more than one without.

title: Seismic zones, flood and cyclone risk for data centres in India (2026)
description: Indian data centre cities by IS 1893 seismic zone, with the 2025 Zone VI map and its reported 2026 withdrawal, record floods in Mumbai, Chennai and Hyderabad, east coast cyclones and CRZ limits.
intro: Most of India’s data centre capacity sits in seismic zone III: Mumbai, Chennai, Pune and Kolkata, with Delhi in zone IV and Bengaluru, Hyderabad and Visakhapatnam in zone II under the IS 1893 (Part 1) town list (2002 edition, zones retained in 2016). A 2025 revision of the code added a Zone VI for the Himalayan arc, but it was reported withdrawn in March 2026, so the 2016 four-zone map applies. Flood risk is the more frequent problem: Mumbai recorded 944 mm of rain in 24 hours in July 2005 and Chennai 1,178.3 mm in November 2015. On the east coast, Cyclone Hudhud crossed Visakhapatnam in 2014 with winds of about 180 km/h.
takeaways: Design to IS 1893 (Part 1):2016; the 2025 edition with Zone VI was reported withdrawn by BIS in March 2026.
Chennai and Visakhapatnam carry cyclone exposure; Mumbai and Chennai carry the record rainfall events.
Near the coast, CRZ 2019 No Development Zones are 50 m or 200 m from the high tide line.

sections.heading: Seismic zones of India’s data centre cities

blocks.text: City zones are from Annex E of IS 1893 (Part 1):2002, and the 2016 edition keeps the four-zone map. Noida and the YEIDA sectors are not listed by name; confirm the zone for a specific site.

sections.heading: The 2025 seismic map and Zone VI

blocks.text: BIS issued IS 1893 (Part 1):2025 around November 2025 with a new Zone VI covering the Himalayan arc. News reports in March 2026 said BIS withdrew it by a gazette notification dated 3 March 2026 after the housing ministry raised cost and consultation concerns, and that the 2016 edition is back in force. We have not seen the gazette notice itself; the withdrawal is as reported.
For a data centre project that means designing to the 2016 edition today and watching for a re-issued revision, which could change the zone for sites near zone boundaries.

sections.heading: Flood history in data centre cities

rows: 944 mm in 24 hours at Santacruz, a city record
1,178.3 mm in the month at Meenambakkam, the all-time November record
About 415 mm widely reported at Meenambakkam; figures for the window differ
324 mm at Ghatkesar; 33 deaths in the city

blocks.text: The BMTPC Vulnerability Atlas of India (third edition, 2019) maps flood, cyclone, wind and earthquake hazard by state and district and is a reasonable first screen before site-specific drainage and plinth studies.

sections.heading: Cyclones on the east coast

blocks.text: Very severe cyclonic storm Hudhud crossed the coast over Visakhapatnam between 12:00 and 13:00 IST on 12 October 2014, with maximum sustained winds of about 180 km/h, a central pressure of 950 hPa and a 1.4 m storm surge at the Visakhapatnam tide gauge. With several gigawatt campuses announced in and around Visakhapatnam, wind loads, surge level and access after landfall belong in the design basis there.

sections.heading: Heat and coastal limits

blocks.text: Chennai’s Meenambakkam station records a mean daily maximum of 37.3°C in May and 37.2°C in June (1991 to 2020 normals), which sets the cooling design point for the city.

The CRZ Notification 2019 sets a No Development Zone of 50 m from the high tide line in densely populated rural coastal areas (CRZ-IIIA) and 200 m in CRZ-IIIB. Coastal sites near Mumbai, Chennai and Visakhapatnam need the CRZ map checked before layout.

title: Water for data centres in India (2026): groundwater NOC, water stress and state rules
description: Indian data centres need a CGWA or state groundwater NOC to draw groundwater, and new industries are barred in over-exploited units. Water use per MW, water-stressed cities and state incentives.
intro: A data centre in India that draws groundwater needs a NOC from the Central Ground Water Authority or the state groundwater authority under the guidelines of 24 September 2020, and no new industry other than an MSME gets one in an over-exploited unit. Whether a data centre counts as industry or as infrastructure, which is treated case by case, has to be confirmed for each site. Anarock puts water use for cooling-tower data centres at about 25.5 million litres per MW per year. SBI names Bengaluru, Chennai and Gurugram as water-stressed data centre metros, and newer state policies push treated wastewater and closed-loop cooling.
takeaways: CGWA 2020 guidelines: NOC needed for groundwater abstraction by industry and infrastructure, with meters, rainwater harvesting and annual audits.
Over-exploited units: no NOC for new industries except MSMEs; 730 of 6,762 units (10.8%) were over-exploited in 2025.
Water use: about 25.5 million litres per MW per year for cooling-tower designs (Anarock).
Karnataka’s Cabinet-approved 2026-31 policy, not yet confirmed as notified, would reimburse treated water costs; Uttar Pradesh’s 2026 policy requires a water assessment before land allocation.

sections.heading: Do data centres need a groundwater NOC in India?

blocks.text: The CGWA guidelines (S.O. 3289(E), 24 September 2020, amended 29 March 2023) require all new, existing and expanding industries, infrastructure projects and mining projects that abstract groundwater to hold a NOC from CGWA or the state or UT groundwater authority, unless exempt. Exemptions cover domestic users, rural drinking water, the armed forces, agriculture and micro and small enterprises drawing less than 10 m3 a day.

rows: No NOC for any new industry except MSMEs; expansion that increases abstraction is not permitted
Location specific; not barred in over-exploited units, but groundwater for construction only if no treated sewage is available within 10 km
An STP is mandatory where groundwater need exceeds 20 m3 a day
Digital flow meter with telemetry and annual calibration
One for 11 to 50 m3 a day; one with a data logger for 51 to 500; two (one with telemetry) above 500
Environmental compensation of ₹20 to ₹200 per m3 for illegal extraction, depending on category and volume

blocks.text: Whether a data centre is an industry or an infrastructure project under these guidelines is not settled in the text we reviewed. In an over-exploited unit it decides whether a NOC is possible at all, so put the question to the authority before committing to the site.

sections.heading: Water stress in data centre cities

blocks.text: The 2025 Dynamic Ground Water Resources Assessment found 730 of 6,762 assessment units (10.8%) over-exploited, concentrated in the north-west, west and south, including Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Telangana and Andhra Pradesh. CGWB-based reporting says every assessment unit in Bengaluru Urban is over-exploited, and Newslaundry reported in April 2026 that most of Bengaluru’s data centres sit in its most water-stressed areas. Check the unit for a specific site on INGRES.
SBI names Bengaluru, Chennai and Gurugram as water-stressed data centre metros and notes that newer rules require water management plans.

sections.heading: How much water does a data centre use in India?

blocks.text: Anarock puts water use at about 25.5 million litres per MW per year for data centres with cooling towers. Down To Earth, an environmental publication, projects India’s data centre water use rising from 150 billion litres in 2025 to 358 billion litres in 2030.

The design choice drives the number. Closed-loop and liquid cooling use far less water than evaporative cooling towers; the government’s September 2026 explainer notes that liquid, adiabatic and immersion cooling are being adopted.

sections.heading: State water rules and incentives

items: Uttar Pradesh (2026): the state agency must assess water availability before allocating land, the developer must get the required permission before using water, and closed-loop cooling and treated wastewater reuse are encouraged.

Karnataka (2026 to 2031): reimburses 100% of treated water costs up to ₹8 lakh a year for 5 years and offers a water usage effectiveness incentive of up to ₹30 lakh a year for 2 years at a WUE of 0.7 to 1.3 litres per kWh, as reported by The News Minute.
NITI Aayog (October 2026): asks states to verify water capacity before clearing data centre projects.

blocks.text: Operators are moving the same way: Digital Edge published a release in February 2026 on an 83 MW solar PPA and recycled water at its Navi Mumbai campus.

title: Power for data centres in India (2026): grid supply, open access, captive and tariffs by state
description: Data centres in India buy power from the discom, through open access or from captive plants. The routes, connection voltages, tariffs for Tamil Nadu and UP, and partly confirmed rates for three more states.
intro: A data centre in India gets its power from the state distribution company (discom), at a voltage set by the state supply code for its contract demand, and can add renewable power through green energy open access or captive plants. Large campuses connect at 110 kV to 230 kV; a bulk consumer of 50 MW or more can connect directly to the inter-state grid. Tariffs differ by state: Tamil Nadu charged ₹7.50/kWh plus ₹608/kVA a month from July 2025, and Uttar Pradesh ₹6.10 to ₹7.10/kVAh for 2026-27. The binding question for a site is rarely the tariff: it is whether the substation and line can deliver the MW, and by when.
takeaways: Three routes: discom supply at high or extra high voltage, green energy open access from 100 kW, and captive or group captive generation (26% ownership, 51% consumption).
Maharashtra classifies data centres as industrial by name; Tamil Nadu bills them as IT services under HT-I; Uttar Pradesh covers notified IT units under HV-2.
Load above 10 MVA usually moves to 110 kV, 132 kV or 220 kV supply from a transmission substation, under each state’s supply code.
The Central Electricity Authority estimates data centre demand of about 17 GW by 2031-32.

sections.heading: The three ways a data centre in India buys power

rows: Supply from the state distribution licensee at HT or EHV
State supply code and the commission’s tariff order
Demand charge per kVA plus energy charge per kWh or kVAh, electricity duty, fuel adjustment
Renewable power bought from a generator or trader and wheeled over the grid
Green Energy Open Access Rules 2022: from 100 kW contracted demand
Transmission, wheeling, cross subsidy surcharge, standby and banking charges
Electricity Rules 2005, Rule 3, as amended in March 2026: at least 26% ownership and 51% consumption
Network charges; no cross subsidy or additional surcharge if the tests are met

blocks.text: Most campuses combine the first route with one of the others: the discom supplies the connection, standby and balance, while open access or captive plants provide renewable energy. A bulk consumer of 50 MW or more may instead connect directly to the inter-state transmission system under CERC’s General Network Access regulations.

sections.heading: At what voltage a data centre connects

blocks.text: Each state supply code ties the connection voltage to contract demand. A 20 MW hall and a 200 MW campus therefore connect very differently.

rows: 11 kV to 3 MVA, 22 kV to 7.5 MVA, 33 kV to 10 MVA (higher limits in metro areas)
Extra high voltage above the 22 and 33 kV limits
11 or 22 kV to 3 or 5 MVA; 33 kV to 10 MVA

132 kV or above, dedicated feeder or LILO
11 kV to 3 MVA; 33 kV to 10 MVA
220 kV feeder from a 220/400 kV substation on request

sections.heading: Electricity tariffs for data centres by state

blocks.text: These are the published rates for the category each state uses for data centres, before fuel adjustment, electricity duty, time-of-day terms and taxes. Units follow each order: some bill energy per kWh, others per kVAh.

rows: HT-I, which covers IT services including data centres

blocks.text: Maharashtra’s numbers need care. MERC revised them in a review order of 25 June 2025, to ₹600/kVA and ₹8.68/kVAh at EHV from 1 July 2025. That order was itself reviewed again, with a further MERC review order reported in March 2026 applying from 1 July 2025, which we have not seen; the rate in force is not confirmed, so check it with MSEDCL before using any of these figures. The Gujarat row is from one small licensee’s order; we did not confirm that the state discoms use the same schedule.
We have not verified current tariffs for Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Haryana or West Bengal for this guide. For those states, the commission’s latest retail supply tariff order is the source.

sections.heading: Which states treat data centres as industry

items: Maharashtra: MERC classified data centres and semiconductor units as industrial to attract high, continuous loads; industrial incentives apply, and data centres using 100% green power get a 10% discount on wheeling charges.
Tamil Nadu: data centres fall under HT-I as IT services, following the state ICT policy definition.
Uttar Pradesh: the HV-2 industrial category covers IT and ITeS units the state notifies by policy.

blocks.text: State data centre policies add power incentives on top. Odisha’s 2022 policy exempts electricity duty for 10 years up to 5 MVA and subsidises 30% of the power bill for five years, capped at ₹2 crore. Uttar Pradesh’s 2026 policy exempts electricity duty for 10 years. Gujarat’s 2026-29 policy offers ₹1 per unit for 20 years to eligible projects of 150 MW or more.

sections.heading: Where power is the constraint

blocks.text: Data centre load is still under 1% of India’s installed power capacity, but it is concentrated. Structure Research reports that the roughly 6 GW of grid capacity MSEDCL allocated to Navi Mumbai data centres is close to fully committed, pushing new builds towards Panvel, Taloja and Rasayani. Crisil estimates that by FY2030 data centre capacity could equal about 60% of Mumbai’s current peak demand and about 80% of Visakhapatnam’s.

The Central Electricity Authority has asked states including Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana and Tamil Nadu to plan resource adequacy for data centre demand. Telangana’s discom chief said in April 2026 that data centres need transmission lines of 132 kV and above.

faqs.question: How do data centres in India get electricity?
faqs.answer: From the state discom, at a voltage set by the state supply code for the contract demand, often supplemented by renewable power bought through green energy open access or from captive plants. Bulk consumers of 50 MW or more can also connect directly to the inter-state grid under CERC rules.

faqs.question: What is the electricity tariff for data centres in India?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state and category. Tamil Nadu charged ₹7.50/kWh plus ₹608/kVA a month from July 2025; Uttar Pradesh charges ₹6.10 to ₹7.10/kVAh plus ₹270 to ₹300/kVA for 2026-27; Telangana ₹6.65 to ₹7.65/kVAh plus ₹500/kVA. Fuel adjustment, duty and taxes are extra.

faqs.question: Are data centres treated as industrial consumers for power?
faqs.answer: In Maharashtra, yes, by name in the MERC tariff order. Tamil Nadu bills them under HT-I as IT services, and Uttar Pradesh under the HV-2 industrial category for notified IT units.

faqs.question: Can a data center in India buy renewable power directly?
faqs.answer: Yes. The Green Energy Open Access Rules 2022 allow any consumer with 100 kW or more of contracted demand to buy renewable power through open access, and captive or group captive plants are allowed if the consumer owns at least 26% and uses at least 51% of the output.

faqs.question: How much power will data centres in India need?
faqs.answer: The Central Electricity Authority estimates about 17 GW of data centre demand by 2031-32, against less than 1% of installed capacity today.

title: Data centre grid connection in India (2026): voltage by load, 220 kV substations, dual grid and GNA
description: How a data centre connects to the grid in India: voltage thresholds in state supply codes, who pays for lines and bays, dual-grid supply, inter-state access from 50 MW and the CERC dual connectivity draft.
intro: A data centre in India connects through the state discom at a voltage its supply code ties to contract demand: in Tamil Nadu 110 kV from 10 to 50 MVA and 230 kV above 50 MVA; in Uttar Pradesh 132 or 220 kV above 10 MVA; in Telangana 132 kV or above beyond 10 to 20 MVA. Dedicated lines, take-off bays and a second source are usually paid for by the consumer. Bulk consumers of 50 MW or more can apply for direct connection to the inter-state transmission system, and a CERC draft of 16 June 2026 would let data centres hold both state and inter-state connections for the same load. The date depends on substation and line work the codes do not time-bound.
takeaways: Above roughly 10 MVA, supply moves from 33 kV to 110, 132 or 220 kV from a transmission substation; the exact threshold is in each state’s supply code.

Telangana’s code makes the consumer pay the full cost of a dedicated feeder, including the take-off arrangement at the substation; Maharashtra charges the extra cost of a second source to the consumer.
Bulk consumers of 50 MW and above may connect directly to the inter-state grid under CERC’s 2022 GNA regulations.
CERC’s June 2026 draft on dual connectivity names data centres; CTUIL supported it, Grid-India and CEA opposed it. It is still a draft.

sections.heading: Connection voltage by contract demand, state by state

blocks.text: Maharashtra, MERC Supply Code 2021:
Tamil Nadu, Supply Code categories: 11 or 22 kV up to 3 or 5 MVA depending on the area network, 33 kV up to 10 MVA, 110 kV from 10 to 50 MVA, and 230 kV above 50 MVA.

Uttar Pradesh, Supply Code 2005 as amended: 33 kV from 3,000 to 10,000 kVA and 132 or 220 kV above 10,000 kVA. Above 10,000 kVA the developer guide calls for a 132 kV feeder from the nearest 132 or 220 kV substation, with a 220 kV feeder from a 220/400 kV substation allowed on request and clearance from the transmission licensee.

sections.heading: Who pays for the line, the bay and a second source

items: Telangana: supply at 132 kV or above is through a dedicated feeder or a loop-in loop-out arrangement decided by the transmission company, and for a dedicated feeder the consumer pays the full cost of the service line, including take-off arrangements at the substation.

Maharashtra: the licensee may provide multiple sources of supply if the consumer asks and it is technically feasible, but the additional cost is borne by the consumer, who may also face additional fixed charges set by the Commission.
Uttar Pradesh: an independent feeder can be given on request if the consumer bears all applicable charges, subject to technical feasibility and availability of a bay and corridor at the substation.

blocks.text: State data centre policies have offered to carry part of this. Tamil Nadu’s 2021 policy promised dual power from the grid for sanctioned loads of 50 MW or more and an additional feeder above 100 MW, for projects incorporated up to 31 March 2026. Uttar Pradesh’s 2021 policy gave dual-grid supply to its first three parks, and its 2026 policy subsidises dual-grid supply for parks. Gujarat’s 2026-29 policy facilitates dual feeders.

sections.heading: How long a connection takes

blocks.text: Maharashtra’s code is the most explicit: supply from the existing network within 7 to 30 days, three months where mains must be extended or augmented, and one year where a new distribution substation is needed. We found no state code that sets a timeline for a new 132 kV or 220 kV bay or line; in practice that depends on the transmission utility approving and building the scheme.

Maharashtra’s State Grid Code shows the planning tests a new load is checked against: the intra-state system must withstand the outage of a 132 kV or 220 kV double-circuit line, a 400 kV single-circuit line or a single interconnecting transformer without curtailing load, and a single 220 kV substation is capped at 500 MVA and a 400 kV substation at 2,000 MVA.

sections.heading: Direct connection to the inter-state grid and the 2026 draft

blocks.text: CERC’s GNA Regulations 2022 let a bulk consumer seeking to connect directly to the inter-state transmission system, with a load of 50 MW and above, apply for General Network Access. A 2023 amendment lets such a consumer share that access with subsidiaries connected at the same point.

On 16 June 2026 CERC published a draft fourth amendment that would let an entity already connected to a state network also connect directly to the inter-state system for the same drawal capacity, with the state transmission utility’s consent. CERC wrote that data centres, green hydrogen plants and smelters may require dual connectivity with round-the-clock, economical power. The nodal agency would grant access only after technical studies. CTUIL supported the proposal; Grid-India opposed it over control-area and scheduling issues, and CEA opposed it as leading to a sub-optimal transmission system. As of 21 November 2026 we had not seen a final notification.

The same memorandum quotes CTUIL saying it has difficulty finalising transmission for about 33 GW of renewable connectivity partly because of uncertainty in bulk loads like green hydrogen and data centres. For a developer, that is the planning gap in one sentence: transmission for a load gets built when the load is credible on paper.

sections.heading: Data centre parks with their own distribution

blocks.text: Maharashtra notified 25 areas, including Navi Mumbai, Panvel, Thane, Chandivali and Marol, where data centre parks can act as deemed distribution licensees, and an October 2025 energy department order lets such parks set up captive renewable plants and distribute within notified zones, as reported by Construction World. Structure Research links the shift to Panvel, Taloja and Rasayani to the near-full 6 GW allocation for Navi Mumbai.

sections.heading: Inspection before energisation

blocks.text: Before an installation is energised, the CEA (Measures relating to Safety and Electric Supply) Regulations 2023 apply. Each state notifies the voltage up to which owners may self-certify. Andhra Pradesh set 33 kV in March 2026: installations above 33 kV are inspected by the Electrical Inspector, and generating units above 10 kW need inspection before commissioning. A draft CEA connectivity standard issued in July 2026 would also bring bulk consumers connected at 33 kV and above under common technical standards, as reported by Indian Infrastructure.

faqs.question: At what voltage does a data centre connect in India?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state supply code and the contract demand. In Tamil Nadu, 110 kV from 10 to 50 MVA and 230 kV above 50 MVA; in Uttar Pradesh, 132 or 220 kV above 10 MVA; in Telangana, 132 kV or above beyond 10 MVA on a common feeder or 20 MVA on a dedicated one; in Maharashtra, extra high voltage above 10 MVA (20 MVA in metro areas).

faqs.question: Who pays for a dedicated 132 kV or 220 kV line to a data centre?
faqs.answer: Usually the consumer. Telangana’s code makes the consumer pay the full cost of a dedicated feeder including take-off at the substation, and Uttar Pradesh gives independent feeders if the consumer bears the charges and a bay is available.

faqs.question: Can a data centre connect directly to the inter-state transmission system?
faqs.answer: Yes, if its load is 50 MW or more: CERC’s GNA Regulations 2022 let bulk consumers apply for direct connection to the inter-state system. A June 2026 CERC draft would also allow dual state and inter-state connection for data centres; it is not final.

faqs.question: What is dual grid supply for a data centre?
faqs.answer: Supply from two independent sources so one outage does not drop the site. Maharashtra allows it on request with the extra cost borne by the consumer; Tamil Nadu’s 2021 and Uttar Pradesh’s data centre policies offered it to large loads and parks.

faqs.question: How long does it take to get a power connection for a data center in India?
faqs.answer: Maharashtra’s code sets one year where a new distribution substation is needed. No state code we found sets a timeline for a new 132 kV or 220 kV bay or line, which depends on the transmission utility building the scheme.

title: Green energy open access for data centres in India (2026): GEOA rules, banking, ISTS waiver and group captive
description: How data centres in India buy renewable power: Green Energy Open Access Rules 2022 (100 kW, 15-day deemed approval, monthly banking), the ISTS waiver phase-out to 2028, and group captive rules amended in March 2026.
intro: Data centres in India buy renewable power mainly through green energy open access and captive or group captive plants. The Green Energy Open Access Rules 2022 open the route to any consumer with 100 kW or more of contracted demand, deem an application approved after 15 days, allow at least monthly banking of at least 30% of consumption, and remove additional surcharge for consumers paying fixed charges. The waiver of inter-state transmission charges for new solar and wind is being phased out, with full charges from July 2028. Captive rules amended in March 2026 keep the 26% ownership and 51% consumption tests and make it easier to hold plants through group companies.
takeaways: Eligibility: 100 kW of contracted demand, which can be met across connections in the same electricity division; no limit for captive consumers.
Charges are limited to transmission, wheeling, cross subsidy surcharge, standby and, since 2023, banking charges; no additional surcharge if fixed charges are paid.
ISTS charges for solar and wind commissioned after 30 June 2025 rise from 25% to 100% by July 2028.
Captive and group captive avoid cross subsidy surcharge and additional surcharge, the largest open access adders, if the 26% and 51% tests are met.

sections.heading: What the Green Energy Open Access Rules 2022 allow

rows: Consumers with contracted demand or sanctioned load of 100 kW and above; no limit for captive consumers
Within 15 days, failing which it is deemed approved; applications through a central nodal agency portal
At least monthly, of at least 30% of the total monthly consumption from the discom
Transmission, wheeling, cross subsidy surcharge and standby charges; no other charges
Cannot rise by more than 50% over 12 years from the surcharge fixed in the year open access is granted
Not applicable to green open access consumers paying fixed charges

blocks.text: A January 2023 amendment raised the cap on standby charges from 10% to 25% of energy charges and added banking charges to the permitted list, as reported by Mercom. States set the banking charge: an MSEDCL commercial circular of September 2024 sets it at 8% of the energy banked.

sections.heading: The inter-state transmission charge waiver and its phase-out

blocks.text: The Ministry of Power extended the waiver of inter-state transmission charges to solar and wind projects commissioned up to 30 June 2025. After that the waiver steps down by commissioning year, running July to June: projects commissioned from 1 July 2025 to 30 June 2026 pay 25% of the charges, 1 July 2026 to 30 June 2027 50%, 1 July 2027 to 30 June 2028 75%, and from 1 July 2028 100%. The same trajectory appears in the ministry’s order for hydro projects. A Ministry of Power office memorandum of 16 April 2026, as reported by PowerPeak Digest, lets projects delayed because transmission was not ready keep a graded waiver if they meet conditions on PPA, connectivity and commissioning dates.
For a data centre signing a long-term renewable contract now, the commissioning date of the generator decides how much of the inter-state charge the contract carries for its life.

sections.heading: Captive and group captive under the 2026 amendment

blocks.text: The Electricity (Amendment) Rules 2026, notified in March 2026, substitute Rule 3 of the Electricity Rules 2005. The tests stay at 26% ownership and 51% of annual generation consumed by captive users. Ownership now counts subsidiaries, the holding company and fellow subsidiaries, and verification moves to NLDC for inter-state cases.

pv magazine India summarises the other changes: a special purpose vehicle is treated as an association of persons whose members can meet the tests together; each user’s consumption is capped at its proportionate ownership share unless it holds 26% or more; and cross subsidy and additional surcharges are not levied pending verification, with carrying cost if the plant later fails the tests.

sections.heading: State green power terms that matter to data centres

items: Maharashtra: green tariff of ₹0.25/kWh over the category tariff for the current control period, and a 10% wheeling discount for data centres using 100% green power; MERC rejected a zero green tariff for round-the-clock green power to data centres.
Gujarat 2026-29 policy: at least 51% renewable power for eligible projects; open access is allowed.
Uttar Pradesh 2026 policy: 50% renewable energy in new data centres by 2030, and transmission and wheeling exemptions of up to 100% depending on the renewable source.
Odisha 2022 policy: 100% reimbursement of transmission and wheeling charges for captive renewable power within the state.

sections.heading: What operators have signed

blocks.text: Digital Edge signed an 83 MW solar power purchase agreement with Hexa Climate for its Navi Mumbai campus, with power from December 2026. Meta, alongside its 168 MW lease at Reliance’s Jamnagar campus, contracted nearly 1 GW of new renewables with CleanMax and Fourth Partner. The Star reported in May 2026 that STT GDC and Nxtra source about 40% of their energy from non-fossil sources.

CERC framed its June 2026 draft on dual connectivity around round-the-clock and economical power for data centres and similar loads, which would let a site draw renewable power over the inter-state grid and firm it from the state network. Nuclear is the longer option: the draft SHANTI Rules of August 2026 would license captive nuclear generation and name data centres as a use. Both are drafts.

faqs.question: What is green energy open access?
faqs.answer: The route under the Green Energy Open Access Rules 2022 that lets a consumer with 100 kW or more of contracted demand buy renewable power from a generator of its choice over the grid, with approval deemed after 15 days and charges limited to those the rules list.

faqs.question: Can data centres use green energy open access in India?
faqs.answer: Yes. Any consumer with 100 kW or more of contracted demand is eligible, and captive consumers have no limit. Data centres in Maharashtra using 100% green power also get a 10% wheeling discount.

faqs.question: What charges apply under green energy open access?
faqs.answer: Transmission, wheeling, cross subsidy surcharge, standby and banking charges. Additional surcharge does not apply if the consumer pays fixed charges, and the cross subsidy surcharge cannot rise by more than 50% over 12 years.

faqs.question: What is group captive power?
faqs.answer: Generation owned jointly by its users. Under Rule 3 of the Electricity Rules 2005, as amended in March 2026, users must together own at least 26% and consume at least 51% of the annual output; meeting the tests avoids cross subsidy and additional surcharges.

faqs.question: When does the ISTS waiver for renewable energy end?
faqs.answer: Solar and wind commissioned up to 30 June 2025 keep the full waiver. Later projects pay 25%, 50% and 75% of the charges in successive July to June years, and 100% from 1 July 2028; an April 2026 memorandum keeps a graded waiver for some projects delayed by transmission.
