title: Open access charges by state (2026): cross subsidy surcharge, additional surcharge and wheeling for data centres
description: What cross subsidy surcharge, additional surcharge, wheeling, transmission, standby and banking charges are, the caps in the 2022 green open access rules, and the state data centre policy waivers we could verify.
intro: A data centre buying power through open access in India pays the network and the discom for the power it no longer buys from them: transmission and wheeling charges for using the wires, a cross subsidy surcharge and often an additional surcharge to compensate the discom, plus standby and banking charges. The Green Energy Open Access Rules 2022 cap what green open access consumers can be charged: no additional surcharge if they pay fixed charges, and a cross subsidy surcharge that cannot rise by more than 50% over 12 years. The figures themselves are set every year in each state commission’s tariff order, and several state data centre policies waive part of them.
takeaways: Cross subsidy surcharge compensates the discom for the cross subsidy it loses when a high-paying consumer leaves; additional surcharge covers its stranded fixed costs.
Green open access consumers paying fixed charges do not pay additional surcharge.
Captive and group captive users meeting the 26% and 51% tests pay neither surcharge.

Data centre policy waivers vary: Uttar Pradesh 2026 up to 100% of transmission and wheeling depending on the renewable source; Odisha 100% for in-state captive renewables; Tamil Nadu’s 2021 concessions closed to new projects in March 2026.

sections.heading: What each open access charge is

rows: Use of the inter-state or intra-state transmission network
CERC for inter-state, the state commission for intra-state
Use of the discom’s distribution network
State commission, in the tariff order
The cross subsidy the discom loses when a consumer buys elsewhere
State commission, under Section 42 of the Electricity Act 2003
The discom’s fixed costs stranded by its obligation to supply
Discom supply when the open access source fails
State commission; capped at 25% of energy charges for green open access after the January 2023 amendment (Mercom)
Storing surplus renewable energy for later use within the month
State commission; MSEDCL sets 8% of energy banked

sections.heading: Caps that apply to green open access

items: Only transmission, wheeling, cross subsidy surcharge, standby and banking charges may be levied; no other charges.
Additional surcharge does not apply to green open access consumers paying fixed charges.
Cross subsidy surcharge cannot rise by more than 50% over 12 years from the year open access is granted.
Cross subsidy and additional surcharges do not apply to green hydrogen or ammonia, or to waste-to-energy supply.

blocks.text: Captive and group captive plants meeting the 26% ownership and 51% consumption tests avoid both surcharges, which is why large consumers prefer them. Under the March 2026 amendment, surcharges are not levied while the tests are being verified, with carrying cost if the plant fails.

sections.heading: What we verified by state

blocks.text: We did not find a single current source listing open access charges for every state, and we have not compiled each commission’s current cross subsidy surcharge for this guide. The table records what we did verify and where to look for the rest.

rows: HT wheeling component of ₹0.62/kVAh (FY 2025-26) and ₹0.60/kVAh (FY 2026-27) in the March 2025 multi-year order, since revised by MERC review orders (current rate not verified); 10% wheeling discount for data centres on 100% green power; banking charge 8%
MERC tariff orders and MSEDCL commercial circulars

2026 data centre policy: transmission and wheeling exemption up to 100% depending on the renewable source; the 2021 policy exempted 50% of transmission and wheeling charges for 25 years on intra-state sale (Invest UP)
UPERC orders; Invest UP for policy benefits
2021 data centre policy: open access charges at 50% and cross subsidy surcharge at 60% (wind) or 70% (solar) of conventional, for projects incorporated up to 31 March 2026
2022 data centre policy: 100% reimbursement of transmission and wheeling charges for captive renewables in the state
OERC orders; OCAC for policy benefits
FY 2026-27 order reportedly caps industrial and commercial cross subsidy surcharge at 20% of the average cost of service

faqs.question: What is cross subsidy surcharge in open access?
faqs.answer: A charge an open access consumer pays the discom for the cross subsidy the discom loses when that consumer buys power elsewhere. The state commission sets it under Section 42 of the Electricity Act 2003; for green open access it cannot rise by more than 50% over 12 years.

faqs.question: What is additional surcharge in open access?
faqs.answer: A charge that covers the discom’s fixed costs stranded by its obligation to supply. Under the Green Energy Open Access Rules 2022 it does not apply to green open access consumers who pay fixed charges.

faqs.question: What are wheeling charges?
faqs.answer: Charges for using the discom’s distribution network to carry power from the generator to the consumer, set in the state tariff order. In Maharashtra the March 2025 multi-year order set the HT wheeling component at ₹0.62/kVAh for FY 2025-26, since revised by review orders (current rate not verified), with a 10% discount for data centres on 100% green power.

faqs.question: Do data centres pay cross subsidy surcharge on captive power?
faqs.answer: Not if the plant meets the captive tests: at least 26% ownership and at least 51% of annual generation consumed by captive users, under Rule 3 as amended in March 2026.

faqs.question: Which states waive open access charges for data centres?
faqs.answer: Uttar Pradesh’s 2026 policy exempts transmission and wheeling up to 100% depending on the renewable source; Odisha’s 2022 policy reimburses them for in-state captive renewables; Tamil Nadu’s 2021 concessions applied to projects incorporated up to 31 March 2026.

title: India data centre power demand to 2032: what CEA and the government project (2026)
description: Official projections of data centre electricity demand in India range from 13.56 GW to 26.3 GW by 2031-32, with CEA at about 17 GW. Why they differ, how they compare with peak demand, and where the load concentrates.
intro: The Central Electricity Authority estimates data centre power demand in India at about 17 GW by 2031-32, the figure the government gave Parliament in August 2026. Other official figures differ: 13.56 GW by 2031-32 was cited in March 2026, and, as reported by Business Standard, the Minister of State for Power told Parliament in July 2026 that AI data centres would add 26.3 GW by 2031-32. Today data centre capacity is under 1% of installed power capacity, against an all-India peak that reached 256.1 GW in April 2026. The load is concentrated: Crisil estimates data centres could equal about 60% of Mumbai’s current peak demand by FY2030.
takeaways: CEA: about 17 GW of data centre demand by 2031-32 (PIB, August 2026).
Government figures range from 13.56 GW to 26.3 GW for the same year, depending on scope and date.
All-India peak demand: 250 GW (May 2024), 256.1 GW (April 2026), and a reported 270.82 GW (May 2026).
Locally the share is large: Crisil puts data centres at about 60% of Mumbai’s and about 80% of Visakhapatnam’s current peak by FY2030.

sections.heading: Estimates disagree: the official numbers side by side

rows: About 17 GW of data centre demand
Central Electricity Authority, in a government reply to the Rajya Sabha (August 2026)
Minister of State for Electronics and IT, citing Ministry of Power data
More than 13.6 GW, and 16.4 GW by 2040
CEA National Generation Adequacy Plan, March 2026
26.3 GW of additional AI data centre load
Minister of State for Power, written reply to Parliament (July 2026)

blocks.text: The figures measure different things: total data centre demand, demand from AI data centres only, or load expected to connect. They also date from different months of a year in which announced projects multiplied. Business Standard reported that the 26.3 GW figure is nearly double the March estimate and is expected to be served primarily by renewable capacity.

sections.heading: How that compares with India’s power system

rows: 256.1 GW (solar 21.5% of supply at the peak)
Data centre share of installed capacity

blocks.text: The Ministry of Power’s year-end review gave 242.49 GW as the FY 2025-26 maximum, while its April 2026 release cites 245.4 GW on 9 January 2026; we use the later figure. The 270.82 GW peak was reported by ANI from ministry posts; we did not find a PIB release for it. CEA’s mid-term review projects the all-India peak above 388 GW by March 2032, as reported by Inc42.

sections.heading: Where the load lands

blocks.text: National shares understate the local effect. Crisil estimates that by FY2030 data centre capacity could equal about 60% of Mumbai’s current peak demand, about 20% of Hyderabad’s and about 80% of Visakhapatnam’s. The Star, citing Asia News Network reporting, said data centres could consume a third of the electricity produced in Mumbai by 2030.

Cushman & Wakefield counted 1,789 MW of operational capacity and 3,860 MW upcoming in the top seven cities in H1 2026, with Mumbai holding 890 MW. Structure Research reports that Navi Mumbai’s roughly 6 GW grid allocation for data centres is close to fully committed.

sections.heading: How planners are responding

items: CEA set up a committee on the operational, policy and regulatory issues of large data centres, their grid impact and cybersecurity, reporting to the National Power Committee (KNN India, October 2026).
CEA asked states including Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana and Tamil Nadu to enhance resource adequacy for data centre demand (ThePrint, April 2026).
CERC’s June 2026 draft would let data centres hold both state and inter-state connections; CTUIL cites uncertainty in data centre loads as one reason transmission planning is stuck.
Former POSOCO chief S.K. Soonee and Prof. P. Pareek have urged CEA to add data centre load characteristics, such as ramps and ride-through, to transmission planning criteria.

blocks.text: Nuclear is part of the government’s answer: in his August 2026 Independence Day address the Prime Minister linked chips, AI and data centres to electricity demand and the SHANTI Act, with a 100 GW nuclear target for 2047.

title: Power study for a data centre site in India: load flow and N-1 against discom, STU and CTU networks
description: What a power study for an Indian data centre site covers: the discom, state and inter-state network, load flow and N-1 tests to state grid code criteria, what data is public, and what only the utility confirms.
intro: A power study for a data centre site in India estimates how many MW each nearby substation can take, at which voltage, and what limits it, by modelling the discom, state transmission (STU) and, for 50 MW and above, inter-state (CTU) network around the site and testing it at N-0 and N-1. The test criteria come from the state grid code: Maharashtra’s requires the system to withstand the loss of a 132 kV or 220 kV double-circuit line, a 400 kV single circuit or a single interconnecting transformer without load curtailment. A screening study tells you where to apply, how much to ask for and which upgrades to expect. Only the discom’s sanction, or the nodal agency’s grant of inter-state access, makes a number firm.
takeaways: The study follows the connection hierarchy: 33 kV discom supply for small halls, 110 to 230 kV STU substations above about 10 MVA, and inter-state access for 50 MW and above.
State grid codes set the N-1 tests and substation limits; Maharashtra caps a single 220 kV substation at 500 MVA and a 400 kV substation at 2,000 MVA.
Public network data in India is thinner than the planning question needs; we found no CTUIL plan naming transmission schemes for the main data centre clusters.
The utility’s own approval is what makes the MW and the date firm.

sections.heading: What the study covers

rows: Discom 33 kV and STU 66 to 400 kV substations, lines and transformers around the site for each study year, with inter-state elements where the load may connect at 400 kV
Each substation that could supply the load at the voltage its contract demand falls under in the state supply code, plus line-in line-out options
Peak and light-load conditions, near-term and later years, with other announced data centre and industrial loads in and out
AC load flow at N-0 and N-1 to the state grid code criteria, for example loss of a 220 kV double-circuit line or an interconnecting transformer
Thermal and voltage limits, the element that binds first and at what MW, and substation capacity limits in the grid code
The augmentation that lifts each limit, an indicative cost range and an energisation range, with the approvals each depends on

blocks.text: The method is the same as a US utility-grade study; what changes is the hierarchy of who studies and approves the connection, and the planning criteria each state sets.

sections.heading: The planning tests a new load must pass

blocks.text: Maharashtra’s State Grid Code 2020 requires the intra-state transmission system to withstand, without load curtailment, the outage of a 132 kV double-circuit line, a 220 kV double-circuit line, a 400 kV single-circuit line or a single interconnecting transformer. The outage of one transformer at a 66 kV or higher substation must not overload the rest, and new substations can be proposed when urban transformers exceed 70% loading. A single substation is capped at 250 MVA at 132 kV, 500 MVA at 220 kV and 2,000 MVA at 400 kV.

For inter-state access, bulk consumers of 50 MW or more apply to the CERC nodal agency under the GNA regulations. CERC’s June 2026 draft amendment would grant GNA to entities seeking dual connectivity, such as data centres, only after the nodal agency carries out technical studies.

sections.heading: What data is public, and what is not

items: Public: state supply codes and grid codes, tariff orders, CERC regulations and drafts, and the transmission utilities’ published plans.

Thin: the CTUIL rolling plan study report we retrieved for 2026-27 does not mention data centres, and we found no CTUIL or Grid-India document naming schemes for the Navi Mumbai, Chennai, Hyderabad or Visakhapatnam clusters.
Moving: CEA set up a committee on data centres and grid stability in 2026, and NITI Aayog has asked states to verify power and water capacity before clearing projects.

blocks.text: That gap is why a screening study in India leans on the substation and line data that can be assembled, the announced loads competing for the same substation, and direct questions to the discom and STU.

sections.heading: Why AI loads change the study

blocks.text: Large AI training loads ramp fast and can drop off the grid in a fault. S.K. Soonee, founding CEO of POSOCO, and Prof. P. Pareek of IIT Roorkee have argued that CEA’s transmission planning criteria should include data centre load characteristics such as IT load, PUE, UPS configuration, ramp rates and ride-through, and flag the risk of gigawatt-scale silent exits causing frequency overshoot. A draft CEA connectivity standard of July 2026 would bring bulk consumers at 33 kV and above under common technical standards.

sections.heading: What makes a number firm

blocks.text: A screening study does not commit a discom or transmission utility to anything. The number becomes firm when the discom sanctions the load and the STU approves the substation and bay works, or, for inter-state access, when the nodal agency grants GNA. The study’s value is in arriving at that application with the right connection point, the right MW and the right questions.

faqs.question: What N-1 criteria apply to a data centre connection in India?
faqs.answer: Each state grid code sets them. Maharashtra’s requires the system to withstand loss of a 132 kV or 220 kV double-circuit line, a 400 kV single-circuit line or a single interconnecting transformer without load curtailment.

title: Diesel generator rules for data centres in India (2026): CPCB IV+, pollution category and PESO diesel storage
description: Which rules govern data centre backup generators in India: CPCB IV+ norms for sets up to 800 kW, older standards above 800 kW, the genset-based pollution category, PESO diesel storage thresholds and Delhi NCR curbs.
intro: Backup generators at an Indian data centre answer to three sets of rules: engine emission norms, the state pollution board’s consent category, and petroleum storage licensing. CPCB IV+ norms, notified as G.S.R. 804(E), apply to new gensets up to 800 kW from 1 July 2023; the 2 to 3 MW sets data centres typically use fall under older standards for engines above 800 kW. Under CPCB’s January 2025 classification, a data centre whose only pollution source is gensets is Orange if it has 1 MVA or more on diesel and Green if on gas. If the diesel is Class B, as is usual (confirm with PESO), storage above 2,500 litres needs a licence and above 25,000 litres a PESO licence.
takeaways: CPCB IV+ (G.S.R. 804(E), as cited by CAQM) covers gensets up to 800 kW from 1 July 2023, through type approval at manufacture.
Sets above 800 kW are covered by the older concentration-based standards.
Genset capacity and fuel decide the pollution category: 1 MVA or more on diesel is Orange; on gas, Green.
If diesel is Class B (usual; confirm with PESO): no licence below 2,500 litres, district licence to 25,000 litres, PESO licence above.

sections.heading: Emission norms for data centre gensets

blocks.text: Revised emission standards for genset engines up to 800 kW were notified by G.S.R. 804(E), as cited by CAQM, and apply to new engines from 1 July 2023. They are enforced at manufacture, through CPCB’s type approval and conformity of production procedure.

rows: Type approval and conformity of production at manufacture
Older standards from 2005: CO 150 mg/Nm3, NMHC 100 mg C/Nm3, PM 75 mg/Nm3, NOx 710 ppm(v)
Stack limits plus state board consent conditions
Noise, diesel sets up to 1,000 kVA

blocks.text: The emission and noise figures for older and larger sets are as tabulated by DieselNet alongside the CPCB standard; check the final gazette text for the version that applies to a given engine.

sections.heading: Pollution category and consent

blocks.text: CPCB’s January 2025 classification says projects such as data centres whose pollution potential comes only from gensets may be classified by genset capacity and fuel. Gensets totalling under 1,000 kVA may not need additional classification. Gensets totalling 1 MVA or more on liquid fuel are Orange (pollution index 60.0); on gaseous fuel, Green (50.5). Separately, building construction of 20,000 sq m or more is Orange.

The category sets consent validity and inspection frequency, and generator buildings appear in environmental clearances for large campuses: one 2025 Maharashtra clearance covered two data centre buildings, two DG buildings and a substation. Gas gensets are therefore a consent question as well as a fuel question.

items.label: Approvals for a data centre in India

sections.heading: Diesel storage under the Petroleum Rules 2002

rows: PESO licence, applied for through the National Single Window System and the PESO portal

blocks.text: PESO lists diesel (HSD) among products that need a licence under the Petroleum Rules 2002. Class B covers flash points from 23°C to below 65°C; diesel is usually treated as Class B, but confirm the class of the fuel specified for the site with PESO before relying on these thresholds.

sections.heading: Delhi NCR and the Graded Response Action Plan

blocks.text: In Delhi NCR, the Commission for Air Quality Management restricts DG set operation as air quality worsens. A CAQM direction places no operating restriction on gensets up to 800 kW that comply with G.S.R. 804(E). Whether larger data centre gensets are exempt as an essential service is not something we could confirm; check the current CAQM directions for the site before relying on generator run hours in a Noida or Gurugram design.

sections.heading: State policy terms for backup power

items: Uttar Pradesh 2026: service FAR extended to 40% for DG sets, DG space outside FAR, and multi-level DG stacking allowed with a fire NOC.
Telangana and Odisha policies list a fuel subsidy for backup power, and Telangana exempts data centres from statutory power cuts, per Cushman & Wakefield’s policy comparison.
Andhra Pradesh: generating units above 10 kW need Electrical Inspector inspection before commissioning under its March 2026 order.

title: National data centre policy India 2026: the 2020 draft, the 2025 consultation and what applies now
description: India has no notified national data centre policy as of November 2026. The 2020 MeitY draft was never adopted and talks reopened in August 2025. What applies instead, and what to watch.
intro: India does not have a notified national data centre policy. The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) published a Draft Data Centre Policy in November 2020, and it was never notified. MeitY reopened consultations in August 2025, and no final policy had been issued when we checked on 21 November 2026. Until one is, national rules for data centres come from infrastructure status (October 2022), the Budget 2026-27 tax holiday for cloud services delivered from Indian data centres, and data protection and localisation law. State policies supply most land, power and capital incentives.
takeaways: The 2020 MeitY draft was never notified; consultations restarted in August 2025.
Data centres with at least 5 MW of IT load have had infrastructure status since 11 October 2022.
The Finance Act 2026 exempts foreign cloud companies that buy data centre services in India, from tax year 2026-27 to tax year 2046-47.
NITI Aayog issued a non-binding Data Centre Evaluation Framework on 14 October 2026.
Capital, land and power incentives still come from state policies.

sections.heading: The 2020 draft and the 2025 consultation

blocks.text: MeitY published the Draft Data Centre Policy in November 2020. It was never notified and never came into effect, so nothing in it binds a developer, a state or a utility.

MeitY reopened consultations on a national policy in August 2025. As reported by BW Legal World at the time, the framework under discussion included four Data Centre Economic Zones, single-window clearance and growth in tier-2 and tier-3 cities. Policy trackers have also reported a tax holiday of up to 20 years for the revised draft. Neither has been published as policy.

sections.heading: What applies nationally while there is no policy

items: Infrastructure status: a data centre in a dedicated building with at least 5 MW of IT load is an infrastructure sub-sector under the Communication category of the Harmonised Master List, notified on 11 October 2022.
Tax holiday: foreign companies that sell cloud services globally using data centre services bought from an Indian data centre are exempt on that income from tax year 2026-27 to tax year 2046-47.
Foreign investment: law firms read the FDI policy as allowing 100% foreign investment under the automatic route in companies engaged only in the data centre business.
Data law: RBI, SEBI, IRDAI and CERT-In rules keep defined data and logs in India; the DPDP Rules 2025 add powers over significant data fiduciaries from May 2027.

items.label: Infrastructure status, tax holiday and DC SEZs

sections.heading: NITI Aayog's Data Centre Evaluation Framework (October 2026)

blocks.text: NITI Aayog's Frontier Tech Hub released a Data Centre Evaluation Framework on 14 October 2026. It asks for a central audit mechanism with MeitY as the nodal ministry, a state-wise data centre approval matrix in each state, a single digital clearance portal, a citation for every incentive (notification, validity and department), and measurement of PUE, WUE and CUE against BIS standards at design stage and after commissioning.

As reported by ThePrint, the framework also asks states to verify power and water capacity before clearing projects and recommends bringing data centres under essential services law. It is guidance. It does not bind states or developers.

sections.heading: What the government says about capacity and power

blocks.text: In a Rajya Sabha reply on 7 August 2026, the government said installed data centre capacity grew from 375 MW in 2020 to about 1,575 MW. It named Mumbai, Navi Mumbai, Chennai, Hyderabad, Bengaluru, Delhi NCR and Jamnagar as the main locations and Andhra Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh and West Bengal as emerging states. It said data centre capacity is less than 1% of installed power capacity and that the Central Electricity Authority estimates data centre power demand at about 17 GW up to 2031-32.

MeitY separately told a parliamentary panel that it maintains no official data on data centre capacity. Treat the 1,575 MW figure as an estimate. Private estimates for mid-2026 range from about 1.6 GW to about 1.8 GW depending on what is counted.

sections.heading: What to watch next

items: Notification of a final national data centre policy, and whether it creates Data Centre Economic Zones.
Rules or conditions issued under the August 2026 amendment to the data centre tax exemption.
DPDP Rules obligations for significant data fiduciaries, due from May 2027.
State renewals: the Tamil Nadu 2021 policy covered projects up to 31 March 2026, and the West Bengal 2021 policy ran for five years from September 2021.

title: Data centre infrastructure status, tax holiday and SEZs in India: central incentives (2026)
description: Central incentives for data centres in India: infrastructure status for 5 MW+ IT load since October 2022, the tax holiday to 2047 for cloud services, FDI rules, and what the SEZ changes do not cover.
intro: At the national level, an Indian data centre gets three things. Since 11 October 2022, a data centre with at least 5 MW of IT load is an infrastructure sub-sector, which eases access to long-term credit. From tax year 2026-27 to tax year 2046-47, foreign companies that sell cloud services worldwide using data centre services bought in India are exempt from Indian tax on that income, under the Finance Act 2026; an amendment easing its conditions passed Parliament in August 2026, with assent and rules still to be confirmed. And law firms read the FDI policy as allowing 100% foreign investment under the automatic route for companies only in the data centre business. We found no central capital subsidy or data centre SEZ scheme in force; capital, land and power incentives come from state policies.
takeaways: Infrastructure status needs a dedicated building and at least 5 MW of IT load.
The tax holiday benefits the foreign cloud company, not the Indian data centre operator, whose profits stay taxable.
An amendment Bill passed by Parliament in August 2026 drops the notification conditions and extends the holiday to leased and operated data centres; confirm assent and rules.
The June 2025 SEZ land relaxations apply to semiconductor and electronics SEZs, not data centres.

sections.heading: Central incentives at a glance

rows: Access to infrastructure lending at lower rates
Data centre in a dedicated building, at least 5 MW IT load
Exemption on a foreign company’s income from data centre services bought in India
Foreign cloud company that does not own or operate the facility and sells to Indian users through an Indian reseller
15% margin on cost where the Indian data centre provider is a related entity
Companies engaged only in the data centre business; land-border countries need approval
Law-firm reading of the FDI policy
Minimum land cut from 50 ha to 10 ha
Semiconductor and electronic component SEZs only

sections.heading: Infrastructure status under the Harmonised Master List

blocks.text: The Ministry of Finance added data centres to the Harmonised Master List of Infrastructure Sub-sectors, under Communication, by a notification dated 11 October 2022. The entry covers a "Data Centre housed in a dedicated/centralized building for storage and processing of digital data applications with a minimum capacity of 5 MW of IT load."
The listing was announced in the Budget 2022-23 speech. Its practical effect is easier access to institutional credit, at lower rates, for qualifying projects.

sections.heading: The tax holiday to 2047 for cloud services delivered from India

blocks.text: The Budget of 1 February 2026 proposed a tax holiday till 2047 for foreign companies that provide cloud services to customers globally using data centre services from India, with services to Indian customers routed through an Indian reseller. It also proposed a 15% safe harbour on cost where the Indian data centre service provider is a related entity. The Minister cited about USD 70 billion of data centre investment underway and about USD 90 billion announced.
The government backgrounder sets the window at tax year 2026-27 to tax year 2046-47 and confirms that the domestic data centre company and the reseller remain taxable on their own profits.

The Finance Act 2026, notified on 30 March 2026, exempts a foreign company’s income "by way of procuring data centre services from a specified data centre", if the foreign company does not own or operate the physical infrastructure, sells to Indian users only through an Indian reseller and files prescribed information. A specified data centre had to be set up under an approved scheme, notified by MeitY, and owned and operated by an Indian company.

The Taxation and Other Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 passed the Lok Sabha on 6 August and the Rajya Sabha on 10 August 2026. It removes the conditions that the foreign company be notified and that the data centre be set up under an approved scheme and notified, and extends the exemption to data centres leased and operated by an Indian company. Check the date of assent and any rules issued under it before relying on the amended conditions.

sections.heading: Foreign investment in data centres

blocks.text: As Khaitan & Co read the FDI policy, 100% foreign investment is allowed under the automatic route in Indian companies or LLPs engaged only in the data centre business. If the company also owns fibre or other telecom assets, the conditions for those sectors apply as well. Investors from countries that share a land border with India need government approval under Press Note 3 of 2020.

sections.heading: SEZs, GIFT City and data embassies

blocks.text: The SEZ (Amendment) Rules 2025, notified on 3 June 2025, cut the minimum contiguous land for semiconductor and electronic component SEZs from 50 ha to 10 ha. They do not apply to data centres, and we found no SEZ amendment specific to data centres as of November 2026.

The Budget 2023-24 speech said the government would facilitate data embassies in GIFT IFSC for countries seeking digital continuity. We found no final notification or treaty on data embassies. Gujarat’s 2026 data centre policy names GIFT City and Dholera as hubs.

For a site in India, Invariant checks how it gets power and the evidence behind that path (the distribution or transmission connection, the open access route, the nearest substations), screens seismic zone, flood history, groundwater status and airport height limits, and maps the central and state approvals the project needs, with the authority behind each one.

title: DPDP Act and data localisation: what it means for data centres in India (2026)
description: India's DPDP Act 2023 restricts transfers by a negative list, not blanket localisation. RBI, SEBI, IRDAI, CERT-In and telecom licences do require data in India. What each means for data centres.
intro: The Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023 does not require all personal data to stay in India. Section 16 lets the central government block transfers to countries it notifies, and keeps stricter sector rules in force. The DPDP Rules 2025, announced on 14 November 2025, phase in over 18 months to May 2027 and let the government require significant data fiduciaries to keep specified data in India. Hard localisation already comes from sector rules: RBI for payment data since 2018, SEBI for regulated entities’ cloud data since 2023, IRDAI for insurance-sector data and logs, and CERT-In for logs. Those rules, more than the DPDP Act, put data center demand on Indian soil today.
takeaways: DPDP Section 16 is a negative list: transfers are allowed unless a country is notified.
Most DPDP Rules obligations apply from May 2027.
RBI requires the entire payment system data to be stored only in India.
SEBI regulated entities must keep cloud data, including DR and logs, within India.
CERT-In requires 180 days of ICT logs kept within India and five years of customer records at data centres.

sections.heading: Which rules keep data in India

rows: The entire data relating to payment systems, including end-to-end transaction details
Data and processing, including DC, DR, near-DR and logs; PaaS and SaaS on MeitY-empanelled data centres with a valid STQC audit
IRDAI Information and Cyber Security Guidelines, 24 April 2023
ICT infrastructure logs, critical and business data (entities other than insurers); insurers under record-keeping regulations
Service providers, data centres, body corporates and government
ICT logs for a rolling 180 days within Indian jurisdiction
Subscriber accounting information and user information, with listed exceptions
Nothing by default; transfers to notified countries can be blocked
Personal data the government specifies on a committee’s recommendation

sections.heading: What the DPDP Act says about cross-border transfer

blocks.text: Section 16(1) of the Act says the central government "may, by notification, restrict the transfer of personal data by a Data Fiduciary for processing to such country or territory outside India as may be so notified." Section 16(2) keeps any other law that provides "a higher degree of protection for or restriction on transfer", which preserves RBI, SEBI and IRDAI localisation.

Section 10 lets the government notify significant data fiduciaries on factors including the volume and sensitivity of data, risk to data principals, sovereignty and integrity of India, electoral democracy, security of the State and public order. They must appoint a Data Protection Officer based in India and an independent data auditor, and run periodic impact assessments and audits. The highest penalty in the Schedule is ₹250 crore, for failing to take reasonable security safeguards.

sections.heading: The DPDP Rules 2025 and the May 2027 date

blocks.text: MeitY announced the DPDP Rules 2025 on 14 November 2025 with an 18-month phased compliance timeline. Consent managers must be Indian companies, data principal requests must be answered within 90 days, and significant data fiduciaries "must also comply with government-specified restrictions on certain categories of data, including localisation where required."

Under the Rules, the government can specify, on a committee’s recommendation, personal data that a significant data fiduciary must process subject to the restriction that it and the traffic data about its flow are not transferred outside India.

In January 2026 Business Standard reported that MeitY was considering cutting the compliance period for key rules from 18 to 12 months. We found no amendment notified, and no significant data fiduciary or restricted-country list notified, as of 21 November 2026.

sections.heading: Sector rules that already require data in India

blocks.text: RBI’s circular of 6 April 2018 requires all system providers to ensure that "the entire data relating to payment systems operated by them are stored in a system only in India", including full end-to-end transaction details. The foreign leg of a transaction may also be stored abroad.

SEBI’s cloud framework of 6 March 2023 says "the data should reside/be processed within the legal boundaries of India", covering DC, DR, near-DR and logs. For PaaS and SaaS, the provider must store or process regulated entity data only within data centres empanelled by MeitY and holding a valid STQC audit status.

IRDAI’s guidelines of 24 April 2023 require regulated entities other than insurers to store all ICT infrastructure logs, critical and business data in India. Insurers keep primary data in India under separate record-keeping regulations. IRDAI amended the guidelines on 6 April 2026; confirm whether the localisation clause changed.

CERT-In’s directions of 28 April 2022 require 6-hour incident reporting and ICT logs kept for a rolling 180 days within Indian jurisdiction. Data centres, VPS, cloud and VPN providers must also keep validated subscriber records for five years or longer.

Telecom licensees may not transfer subscriber accounting information or user information outside India, with exceptions for roaming and certain subscribers, under clause 39.23(viii) of the Unified Licence.

sections.heading: What this means for data centre demand and design

items: Banks, payment companies, insurers and securities firms need primary and disaster recovery capacity inside India, often in two different seismic and flood zones.
Operators that want SEBI-regulated PaaS and SaaS workloads need MeitY empanelment and STQC audit status for the facility.
Log retention, incident reporting and customer records are operating duties for the data centre itself, not only for its tenants.
The DPDP Act alone does not force localisation today. Watch for significant data fiduciary notifications and any restricted-country list from May 2027.

blocks.text: This page summarises public rules and is not legal advice.

faqs.answer: Not by default. Section 16 allows transfers unless the government notifies a country as restricted, and keeps stricter sector rules such as RBI’s in force.

faqs.question: When do the DPDP Rules 2025 come into force?
faqs.answer: In phases over 18 months from November 2025. Most obligations, including those on significant data fiduciaries, apply from May 2027.

faqs.question: Do payment companies have to store data in India?

title: Data centre policy India 2026: state data centre policies compared (power, land, incentives, status)
description: Which Indian states have a data centre policy in 2026, which have lapsed, and what each offers on capital subsidy, power tariff, stamp duty and open access. A dated state by state table with sources.
intro: India has no notified national data centre policy, so the incentives that change a project’s cost come from states. As of 21 November 2026, Uttar Pradesh (2026), Gujarat (2026 to 2029), Maharashtra (IT/ITES Policy 2023 and the Green Data Centre Parks policy amended in June 2026), Andhra Pradesh (4.0, 2024 to 2029) and Odisha (2022, validity not stated) have data centre policies or chapters, Karnataka’s 2026 to 2031 policy was approved by cabinet in September 2026, and Haryana’s 2026 policy was reported notified in May 2026. Tamil Nadu’s 2021 policy covered data centres incorporated up to 31 March 2026 and West Bengal’s 2021 policy ran for five years from September 2021; we found no successor to either. Telangana still points to its 2016 policy.
takeaways: Invest India counted 11 states with dedicated data centre policies as of September 2026.
Eligibility thresholds differ widely: 150 MW of IT load in Gujarat, ₹500 crore of fixed assets in Tamil Nadu, above 2 MW for UP units.
Green power conditions are spreading: at least 51% in Gujarat and Maharashtra parks, 30% in Tamil Nadu’s 2021 policy.

Uttar Pradesh’s 2026 order notifies data centres as essential services under ESMA, and Gujarat’s 2026 policy does the same according to a law-firm summary; West Bengal’s 2021 policy did, but its term has ended.
Mumbai holds about half of top-seven-city operational capacity (Cushman & Wakefield, H1 2026), so Maharashtra’s policy matters most in practice.

sections.heading: Essential service status

blocks.text: Uttar Pradesh’s 2026 government order notifies data centres under ESMA as essential services. Gujarat’s 2026 policy treats data centre operations as an essential service under the Gujarat Essential Services Maintenance Act, 1972, according to Cyril Amarchand Mangaldas; we have not seen the notified resolution. West Bengal’s 2021 policy says data centre organisations "shall be classified under ‘Essential Services’", though that policy’s five-year term has ended. Haryana’s 2026 policy has been reported to grant essential service status.
NITI Aayog’s October 2026 framework recommends bringing data centres under essential services law nationally. It is guidance.

sections.heading: Lapsed, replaced and unclear policies

items: Tamil Nadu: the 2021 policy applies to data centres incorporated from 1 April 2021 until 31 March 2026. We found no successor as of 21 November 2026.

West Bengal: the 2021 policy was operative for five years or until replaced, which ran to about September 2026. In May 2026 the state BJP president said the government was working on a new data centre policy.
Uttar Pradesh: the 2026 policy repealed the 2021 policy (First Amendment 2022). Holders of a Letter of Comfort under the old policy keep their admissible benefits.
Telangana: the 2016 policy is the latest dedicated policy we found. Officials cite a target of about 5 GW by 2029 (Deccan Chronicle) or 2030 (Commissioner of Industries, reported by ANI).
Karnataka: the 2022-27 policy is being replaced by the 2026-31 policy, whose gazette notification we had not seen.

sections.heading: Which state is best for a data centre?

blocks.text: It depends on size and location more than on headline incentives. Gujarat’s policy only admits projects of 150 MW or more. Uttar Pradesh has a band for units above 2 MW. Maharashtra holds about half of India’s operational capacity, with Mumbai at 890 MW in mid-2026, so most interconnection and cable landing density is there, but Structure Research reports that the grid allocation for Navi Mumbai data centres is close to used up.

Check three things before choosing on incentives: whether the policy is in force on the date your project is registered, whether your load and investment clear its threshold, and whether the power path to the site can deliver the MW on your date.

For a site in any Indian state, Invariant checks how it gets power and the evidence behind that path (the distribution or transmission connection, the open access route, the nearest substations), screens seismic zone, flood history, groundwater status and airport height limits, and maps the central and state approvals the project needs, with the authority behind each one.

title: Uttar Pradesh data centre policy 2026: parks, capital subsidy, power incentives and the 2021 policy
description: The UP Data Centre Policy 2026 runs five years from notification: interest subsidy up to ₹50 crore for parks, capital subsidy up to ₹20 crore for units, 10-year electricity duty exemption and wheeling relief.
intro: Uttar Pradesh replaced its 2021 data centre policy with the UP Data Centre Policy 2026, which is in effect for five years from its notification in 2026. It targets more than ₹2 lakh crore of investment and sorts projects into parks of at least 40 MW, units above 2 MW and below 40 MW, edge sites and centres of excellence. Parks can get an interest subsidy up to ₹50 crore and a dual-grid subsidy; units can get a capital subsidy up to ₹20 crore. Electricity duty is exempt for 10 years, and transmission and wheeling charges can be exempted up to 100% depending on the renewable source. Most of the state’s data center capacity is in Noida and Greater Noida.
takeaways: The 2026 policy repealed the 2021 policy; Letter of Comfort holders under the old policy keep their benefits.
Land subsidy is 25% in Madhyanchal and Paschimanchal and up to 50% in Bundelkhand and Purvanchal.
Stamp duty is 100% exempt on purchase or lease from government authorities.
The policy aims for 50% renewable energy in new data centres by 2030.
Projects above ₹200 crore go to the empowered committee or the cabinet.

sections.heading: Incentives by segment

items: Parks of 40 MW or more: interest subsidy up to ₹50 crore and a subsidy for dual-grid power.
Units above 2 MW and below 40 MW: capital subsidy up to ₹20 crore.

All segments: land subsidy of 25% in Madhyanchal and Paschimanchal and up to 50% in Bundelkhand and Purvanchal; 100% stamp duty exemption on purchase or lease from government authorities and 50% on the second transaction (park to unit), granted against a bank guarantee released at commercial operation; 100% electricity duty exemption for 10 years.
Boosters: an AI Compute Booster and a green operations booster, and encouragement for Tier III and Tier IV facilities.

blocks.text: The government order adds a non-financial chapter covering essential service status under ESMA, water supply, building norms and electricity supply. Projects above ₹200 crore are approved by the empowered committee or the cabinet.

sections.heading: Power: electricity duty, wheeling and dual grid

blocks.text: Electricity duty is fully exempt for 10 years. Transmission and wheeling charges can be exempted up to 100%, with the share depending on the renewable source. Parks get a dual-grid power subsidy, and the state aims for 50% renewable energy in new data centres by 2030.
Incentives do not create grid capacity. A park still needs a connection the distribution company or transmission utility can deliver on its date.

sections.heading: What the 2021 policy offered, and who keeps it

blocks.text: The 2021 policy targeted 250 MW, ₹20,000 crore and at least three private parks. It offered a capital subsidy of 7% up to ₹10 crore, an interest subsidy of 60% for 7 years up to ₹50 crore per park, land subsidy of 25% or 50% up to ₹75 crore, stamp duty of 100% on the first transaction and 50% on the second, electricity duty exemption for 10 years, dual grid for the first three parks with the Energy Department bearing the cost of the second grid, and 50% transmission and wheeling exemption for 25 years on intra-state sale.

A 2022 amendment was reported to raise the targets to 900 MW, ₹30,000 crore and eight parks. The 2026 policy repeals the 2021 policy and its amendment; entities that hold a Letter of Comfort under it keep their admissible benefits.

sections.heading: Where Uttar Pradesh’s data centres are

blocks.text: Noida is the state’s data centre market. Cushman & Wakefield counted 156 MW of operational capacity in 12 data centres in Noida in mid-2026, with 21 MW under construction, 223 MW planned and 1,247 MW at an early stage. Delhi NCR as a whole had 183 MW operational.

title: Maharashtra data centre policy 2026: Green Integrated Data Centre Parks, IT/ITES Policy 2023 incentives and power
description: Maharashtra covers data centres in its IT/ITES Policy 2023 and its Green Data Centre Parks policy, expanded to 20 parks in June 2026: stamp duty, electricity duty and a ₹1 per unit tariff subsidy.
intro: Maharashtra has no standalone data centre policy. Data centres are covered by the IT/ITES Policy 2023, adopted by Government Resolution on 27 June 2023 for five years, and by the Integrated Green Data Centre Parks policy of October 2024, which a Government Resolution of 9 June 2026 expanded from 3 to 20 parks across the state. The IT policy gives 100% stamp duty exemption, a permanent electricity duty exemption for registered data centres and a ₹1 per unit tariff subsidy for five years outside Zone I. According to trade reports of the June 2026 resolution, the parks policy cuts the green power requirement to 51% and extends the ₹1 per unit subsidy to 10 or 20 years for parks investing ₹30,000 crore or ₹60,000 crore. Mumbai and Navi Mumbai hold about half of top-seven-city operational data center capacity.
takeaways: Data centres may be set up in any zone under the IT/ITES Policy 2023.
The June 2026 amendment raised the number of green parks from 3 to 20 and applies retrospectively.
At ₹60,000 crore or more, parks also get an industrial promotion subsidy of 75% of eligible fixed capital investment.
Navi Mumbai’s grid allocation for data centres is reported to be nearly used up, pushing new builds to Panvel, Taloja and Rasayani.

sections.heading: Integrated Green Data Centre Parks after the June 2026 amendment

blocks.text: According to PowerPeak Digest, a cabinet sub-committee approved changes on 22 April 2026, and a Government Resolution of 9 June 2026 put them into effect. The number of parks rose from 3 to 20 and can be anywhere in the state. The green power share for core operations fell from 100% to 51%. The ₹1 per unit tariff subsidy runs for 10 years at ₹30,000 crore of investment, or 20 years at ₹60,000 crore or more. At ₹60,000 crore or more, parks also get an industrial promotion subsidy of 75% of eligible fixed capital investment and a 4% interest subsidy up to ₹25 crore a year for 10 years. Owner, developer and unit investment count together, and the changes apply retrospectively.

blocks.text: Mumbai had 890 MW of operational capacity in mid-2026, about 50% of the top seven Indian cities, with 281 MW under construction and 1,445 MW planned. Thane-Belapur Road alone held 675 MW.

Structure Research reports that MSEDCL has allocated about 6 GW of grid capacity to Navi Mumbai data centres and that committed and under-construction capacity is approaching that level. New builds are moving to Panvel, Taloja and Rasayani, where separate substations can be built.

title: Tamil Nadu data centre policy: the 2021 policy after 31 March 2026, incentives and status
description: Tamil Nadu's Data Centre Policy 2021 covered data centres incorporated up to 31 March 2026, with a ₹500 crore minimum and 30% renewable power. We found no successor as of November 2026.
intro: Tamil Nadu’s Data Centre Policy 2021 came into force on 23 November 2021 and applies to data centres incorporated from 1 April 2021 until 31 March 2026. Incentives needed eligible fixed assets of at least ₹500 crore and at least 30% renewable energy, and included a 100% electricity tax subsidy for five years, open access charges at 50%, a concessional cross subsidy surcharge and dual grid supply for loads of 50 MW or more. The policy is administered by ELCOT. As of 21 November 2026 we found no successor policy, so a data center project incorporated after 31 March 2026 should confirm its position with the state before relying on these terms.

Captive data centres were excluded.
Loads of 50 MW or more got power from two grids, and loads above 100 MW an additional feeder.
Chennai had 214 MW operational in mid-2026, about 12% of the top seven cities.

title: Gujarat data centre policy 2026-29: 150 MW threshold, ₹1 per unit tariff subsidy and essential service status
description: The Viksit Gujarat Data Centre Policy 2026-29, launched 9 July 2026, targets 7.5 GW: 150 MW minimum IT load, 51% renewable power, ₹1 per unit for 20 years and 20 years of electricity duty relief.
intro: Gujarat launched the Viksit Gujarat Data Centre Policy 2026-29 on 9 July 2026, with targets of 7.5 GW and ₹6 lakh crore of investment. It is in force for three years from notification, extendable, and incentives stop once 7.5 GW is reached. Only projects with an approved IT load of at least 150 MW and at least 51% renewable power qualify. Incentives include a ₹1 per unit power tariff subsidy for 20 years, 100% electricity duty reimbursement for 20 years, an interest subsidy of up to 4% for 10 years, stamp duty relief and SGST reimbursement, capped at 75% of eligible fixed capital investment. Cyril Amarchand Mangaldas reports that the policy makes data center operations an essential service under the Gujarat Essential Services Maintenance Act, 1972. These terms are as reported by tele.net and Cyril Amarchand Mangaldas; we have not seen the notified government resolution.

title: Karnataka data centre policy: Sustainable Data Centre Policy 2026-31 and the 2022-27 policy
description: Karnataka approved a Sustainable Data Centre Policy 2026-31 in September 2026: ₹1,300.45 crore outlay, 1 GW target, PUE incentive up to ₹20 crore and parks at Hoskote, Mangaluru and Mysuru.
intro: Karnataka’s cabinet approved a Sustainable Data Centre Policy 2026-31 in September 2026, with an outlay of ₹1,300.45 crore and a target of 1 GW by 2031. It pays for efficiency rather than size: an incentive of up to ₹20 crore for a PUE of 1.00 to 1.20 sustained for three years, water use reimbursements and support for treated water. It plans parks at Hoskote, Mangaluru and Mysuru on 30 plus 30 year leases with dual-grid power. We had not seen the gazette notification as of 21 November 2026. The earlier Data Centre Policy 2022-27 gave capital, land and stamp duty support to data center projects outside Bengaluru.
takeaways: The 2026-31 policy ties its largest incentive to measured PUE, not to MW.
Water use effectiveness of 0.7 to 1.3 litres per kWh earns up to ₹30 lakh a year for two years.
Projects above ₹3,000 crore can get custom packages, including for cable landing stations and desalination.
Bengaluru had 162 MW operational in mid-2026.

title: Andhra Pradesh data centre policy 4.0 (2024-29): mega project packages and Visakhapatnam
description: Andhra Pradesh’s Data Center Policy 4.0 was reported as notified in late 2024 for five years. Mega projects get tailor-made packages; in August 2026 the state cleared four projects totalling 3,498 MW.
intro: Andhra Pradesh’s Data Center Policy 4.0 (2024-29) was reported as notified in late 2024 (14 November according to TeamLease RegTech; another source gives 4 December, and the GO number is unconfirmed), valid for five years, with incentives set through operational guidelines. Mega projects above ₹5,000 crore or 50 MW get tailor-made packages through project-specific government orders. In August 2026 the state cleared four projects worth ₹2.83 lakh crore and 3,498 MW under the policy. Google’s first India AI hub, about USD 15 billion over 2026 to 2030, is in Visakhapatnam, where more than 4 GW is announced or at an early stage.
takeaways: Standard incentives are in the operational guidelines; large projects negotiate project-specific orders.
The August 2026 approvals included a 1,000 MW ReNew project in Anakapalli with incentives of up to ₹14,400 crore.
Crisil estimates Visakhapatnam data centre capacity could equal about 80% of the city’s current peak power demand by FY2030.

title: West Bengal data centre policy 2021: incentives, essential services status and what happens after 2026
description: West Bengal's Data Centre Policy 2021, notified 6 September 2021 for five years, gives stamp duty and electricity duty relief, essential services status and dual grid power. Its term ended around September 2026.
intro: West Bengal’s Data Centre Policy 2021 was notified on 6 September 2021 and is operative for five years or until replaced, so its term ran to about September 2026. It gives 100% stamp duty and registration fee exemption, a five-year electricity duty waiver, industrial treatment of data centre electricity, dual grid power and classification of data centres as essential services. In May 2026 the state BJP president said the government was working on a new data centre policy; we found no successor as of 21 November 2026. Kolkata had 22 MW of operational data center capacity in mid-2026.
takeaways: The 2021 policy classifies data centres as essential services (clause 5.3).
Data centres get FAR of 3.0 plus 1.0 purchasable and up to 60% ground coverage.
Cushman & Wakefield reports a cable landing station under construction at Tajpur; other sources conflict.

title: Data centres in Mumbai and Navi Mumbai (2026): capacity, sub-markets, power and land
description: Mumbai holds about half of India’s live data centre capacity: 890 MW in H1 2026, most of it on Thane-Belapur Road in Navi Mumbai, where grid allocation and land are now the binding limits.
intro: Mumbai is India’s largest data centre market. Cushman & Wakefield counted 890 MW of operational capacity in the Mumbai Metropolitan Region in H1 2026, about 50% of the top seven cities, with 281 MW under construction and 1,445 MW planned. Most of it sits on Thane-Belapur Road in Navi Mumbai; the city has 13 cable landing stations. The constraint has moved from demand to power: about 6 GW of grid capacity allocated to Navi Mumbai data centres is close to fully committed, and new builds are moving to Panvel, Taloja and Rasayani.
takeaways: Mumbai had 890 MW operational, 281 MW under construction and 1,445 MW planned in H1 2026 (Cushman & Wakefield). Savills counts 846 MW IT. Both put Mumbai at roughly half of India.
Thane-Belapur Road alone holds 675 MW at 4.4% vacancy. Powai and Chandivali serve interconnection; Panvel, Taloja and Palava are where large new campuses go.
Structure Research reports that the roughly 6 GW grid allocation for Navi Mumbai data centres is close to committed. Power evidence is the first check on any Mumbai site.
Navi Mumbai International Airport opened to commercial flights on 25 December 2025, which adds a second set of height limits over Navi Mumbai clusters.

blocks.text: Estimates differ by method. Cushman & Wakefield counts colocation and hyperscale cloud in the top seven cities and leaves out captive facilities. Savills counts IT load across segments. Anarock gives 812 MW IT across 54 facilities for the region. Use one publisher consistently when comparing periods.

Mumbai took about 83% of top-seven additions in H1 2026 (148 MW) and Cushman & Wakefield expects the city to pass 1 GW of operational capacity by the end of 2026. About 95% of India’s international bandwidth is handled in the region.

sections.heading: Sub-markets: Thane-Belapur Road, Powai, Panvel, Taloja and Palava

rows: 241 MW under construction, 995 MW planned, 2,286 MW early stage

blocks.text: Thane-Belapur Road is the hyperscale core, built on MIDC’s TTC industrial area plots close to the city’s landing stations. Powai and Chandivali, in the city, carry interconnection and enterprise demand; Equinix opened MB3 there in April 2026 with over US$95 million of initial investment. Anarock names Dombivali and Taloja as the emerging lower-cost hyperscale corridor.

Large campuses now go further out. Yotta’s NM1 at Panvel runs 52 MW in a park it says can scale to 1 GW. AdaniConneX lists 1,000 MW of potential in Navi Mumbai, and CoreWeave has agreed to take 240 MW at its Taloja campus from mid-2028. Digital Edge plans 400 MW across its Navi Mumbai campus. STT GDC broke ground at Palava with 50 MW on 46 acres, scalable to about 400 MW.

sections.heading: Power: the Navi Mumbai allocation and what comes next

blocks.text: Structure Research reports that MSEDCL has allocated about 6 GW of grid capacity to Navi Mumbai data centres and that committed and under-construction capacity is approaching that figure. New builds are moving to Panvel, Taloja and Rasayani, where separate substations can be built. The same report notes a Maharashtra framework from October 2025 that lets data centre parks generate and distribute their own power.

Crisil estimates that by FY2030 data centre capacity could equal about 60% of Mumbai’s current peak power demand. That is the scale problem a new site has to answer: a will-serve letter for a few MW is easy, a firm date for 100 MW or more needs a named substation, a transmission plan and a connection agreement.

Under MERC’s Supply Code, 33 kV supply covers contract demand up to 10,000 kVA, or 20,000 kVA in a Metropolitan Area or on an express feeder; larger loads connect at extra high voltage. A connection that needs a new distribution substation has a one-year standard, and a second independent source is available only if technically feasible and at the consumer’s cost.

MERC’s March 2025 tariff order put data centres in the HT industrial category, with industrial rebates, and a 10% wheeling discount for data centres on 100% green power. Construction World reports that Maharashtra notified 25 areas, including Navi Mumbai and Panvel, for deemed distribution licences for data centre parks in May 2025.

Maharashtra’s IT/ITES Policy 2023 gives registered data centres a permanent electricity duty exemption and a Rs 1 per unit tariff subsidy for 5 years outside Zone I. According to trade reports of the 9 June 2026 government resolution, the Integrated Green Data Centre Parks policy now requires parks to source at least 51% green power, and the Rs 1 per unit subsidy runs 10 years at Rs 30,000 crore of investment or 20 years at Rs 60,000 crore or more.

sections.heading: Land: prices, parcels and approvals

blocks.text: Anarock benchmarks land at Rs 35 to 60 crore per acre for 5 to 10 MW parcels in Mumbai’s suburbs and Rs 3 to 10 crore per acre for 100 to 500 MW parks such as Navi Mumbai. Recent deals show the spread. STT GDC paid Rs 282 crore for 3.48 acres with a building in the TTC industrial area in May 2026. AWS bought 38.18 acres from Lodha near Mumbai for about Rs 450 crore in 2024.

A typical Navi Mumbai route is a plot in a MIDC industrial area followed by state environmental clearance for the building. Nxtra’s Mahape expansion, two data centre buildings, two generator buildings and a substation with 76,930 sq m of built-up area, received its clearance from SEIAA Maharashtra on 21 November 2025.
Maharashtra’s IT/ITES Policy 2023 exempts stamp duty on land for new or expanded data centres and lets data centres locate in any zone.

sections.heading: Site risks in Mumbai

items: Seismic: Mumbai and Thane are Zone III (zone factor 0.16) under the IS 1893 (Part 1) town list (2002 edition, zones retained in 2016). The 2025 revision that added a Zone VI was withdrawn in March 2026, so design follows the 2016 edition.
Flood: Santacruz recorded 944 mm of rain in 24 hours on 26 July 2005. Low-lying plots near creeks and nullahs need a site-level drainage and flood check.

Airports: sites within 20 km of an aerodrome reference point (56 km for instrument airports) need an AAI height NOC above the colour-coded zoning map. Navi Mumbai International Airport began commercial flights on 25 December 2025.

blocks.text: Invariant checks the evidence behind a site’s power (the DISCOM or transmission connection, the open access route, the nearest substations and what else is queued on them), screens seismic zone, flood history, groundwater status and airport height limits, and lists the central and state approvals the project needs with the authority behind each one. In Mumbai the first question is which substation serves the plot and how much of its allocation is already committed.

title: Data centres in Chennai (2026): capacity, Ambattur and Siruseri, policy status and flood risk
description: Chennai had 214 MW of operational data centre capacity in H1 2026 (Cushman & Wakefield), mostly in Ambattur and Siruseri, with cable landings, high vacancy and a state policy whose window closed on 31 March 2026.
intro: Chennai is India’s second cable-landing city and its second or third data centre market depending on the count. Cushman & Wakefield counted 214 MW operational in H1 2026 across 18 facilities, about 12% of the top seven cities, with 26.7% colocation vacancy after a run of new supply. Savills counts 320 MW IT. Most capacity is in Ambattur in the west and Siruseri on the OMR corridor. Tamil Nadu’s Data Centre Policy 2021 covered projects incorporated up to 31 March 2026, and we found no successor policy as of November 2026.
takeaways: Chennai had 214 MW operational, 55 MW under construction and 313 MW planned in H1 2026 (Cushman & Wakefield). Savills counts 320 MW IT; Anarock 298 MW IT.
Colocation vacancy was 26.7% in H1 2026, against 7.9% in Mumbai. Siruseri vacancy was 41.7%.
Tamil Nadu’s 2021 policy applied to data centres incorporated from 1 April 2021 to 31 March 2026. Check the status of any incentive before relying on it.
Flood risk is a site-level question: Meenambakkam recorded 1,178.3 mm in November 2015, its all-time November record.

blocks.text: Counts differ by method: Cushman & Wakefield counts colocation and hyperscale cloud and excludes captive sites; Savills counts IT load across segments; Anarock gives 298 MW IT across 25 facilities and forecasts 900 MW by 2030.

High vacancy reflects recent supply, not weak fundamentals. Cushman & Wakefield notes a large neocloud GPU deployment in the city in H1 2026, and JLL says Chennai accounted for 50% of India’s H1 2026 additions in its count.

sections.heading: Sub-markets: Ambattur, Siruseri and the Sriperumbudur corridor

rows: 42 MW under construction, 124 MW planned, 548 MW early stage

blocks.text: Ambattur, in the city’s west, is where the next wave of large buildings is going. CapitaLand’s Ambattur facility, about 34 MW IT, is due by the end of 2026. Lumina CloudInfra, now owned by AirTrunk, planned a 216 MW hub on 16 acres there. Siruseri hosts Equinix CN1, opened in September 2025 with 800 cabinets in phase one, and facilities from STT GDC and Sify.

Anarock identifies the Oragadam industrial belt and the Parandur-Sriperumbudur corridor as the emerging zone, with larger and cheaper land. Digital Connexion, the Reliance, Brookfield and Digital Realty joint venture, runs a 100 MW campus in Chennai.

sections.heading: Power and the Tamil Nadu policy after March 2026

blocks.text: The 2021 policy set a minimum investment of Rs 500 crore and required at least 30% renewable power for incentives. It offered a 100% electricity tax subsidy for 5 years, open access charges at 50% of the conventional rate, a concessional cross subsidy surcharge, and supply from two grids for loads of 50 MW or more with an additional feeder above 100 MW.

Under the Tamil Nadu Supply Code, loads above 10 MVA up to 50 MVA connect at 110 kV and loads above 50 MVA at 230 kV. TNERC’s tariff order of June 2025 places data centres in HT-I as IT services, at Rs 7.50 per kWh and Rs 608 per kVA per month from 1 July 2025; check for later inflation-linked revisions.

The policy applied to data centres incorporated from 1 April 2021 until 31 March 2026. Projects incorporated after that date should not assume these terms apply. Confirm with ELCOT and the Guidance Tamil Nadu single window what is available now, and get it in writing.

sections.heading: Land in Chennai

blocks.text: Anarock’s benchmarks put land for 10 to 30 MW facilities at Rs 5 to 20 crore per acre and large park parcels, including outer Chennai, at Rs 3 to 10 crore per acre. Lumina’s 16 acres in Ambattur were reported at over Rs 500 crore in January 2026.

SIPCOT and ELCOT industrial land and private land follow different routes. Whether a separate land-use conversion is needed depends on the parcel; confirm it with the allotting agency or district authority before signing.

sections.heading: Site risks in Chennai: flood, cyclone and water

items: Flood: Meenambakkam recorded 1,178.3 mm in November 2015, the all-time November record. Cyclone Michaung brought very heavy rain on 3 and 4 December 2023; reported totals vary by station and window.
Seismic: Chennai is Zone III (zone factor 0.16) under the IS 1893 (Part 1) town list (2002 edition, zones retained in 2016).
Heat: the 1991 to 2020 mean daily maximum at Meenambakkam is 37.3 degrees C in May, which sets the cooling design point.
Water: SBI flags Chennai, Bengaluru and Gurugram as water-stressed data centre metros. Groundwater abstraction needs a CGWA or state NOC, and over-exploited units restrict new industrial abstraction.

blocks.text: Invariant checks the evidence behind a site’s power (the DISCOM or transmission connection, the open access route, the nearest substations and what else is queued on them), screens seismic zone, flood history, groundwater status and airport height limits, and lists the central and state approvals the project needs with the authority behind each one. In Chennai, plot elevation and drainage relative to the 2015 and 2023 flood extents come before anything else.

title: Data centres in Hyderabad (2026): capacity, the southern ORR corridor, hyperscalers and power
description: Hyderabad had 151 MW of operational data centre capacity in H1 2026 and the second largest pipeline in India, led by AWS and Microsoft campuses south of the city around Chandanvelly and Shamshabad.
intro: Hyderabad has India’s second-largest data centre pipeline after Mumbai. Cushman & Wakefield counted 151 MW operational in H1 2026, about 8% of the top seven cities, but 668 MW planned and 18% of all upcoming supply to 2030, second only to Mumbai. AWS has run a region here since 2022, and Microsoft formally launched its India South Central region on 21 September 2026 (trade press reported general availability in August). Growth is concentrated south of the city along the outer ring road. The latest dedicated Telangana policy we found is the Data Centres Policy 2016; officials have cited about 5 GW by 2029 or 2030.
takeaways: Hyderabad had 151 MW operational, 42 MW under construction and 668 MW planned in H1 2026 (Cushman & Wakefield).
South Hyderabad holds 92 MW at 0% vacancy, with 1,758 MW at early stage. West Hyderabad (HITEC City, Gachibowli) holds 59 MW.

blocks.text: Baselines conflict. City figures from Cushman & Wakefield and Knight Frank are about 151 MW; figures quoted by Telangana officials are higher, and their basis is not stated.

sections.heading: Sub-markets: the southern ORR belt, HITEC City and Bharat Future City

rows: 39 MW under construction, 634 MW planned, 1,758 MW early stage

blocks.text: The southern outer ring road belt from Maheshwaram through Shamshabad and Tukkuguda is the primary hyperscale corridor, per Anarock. Microsoft announced sites at Chandanvelly, Ellikatta and Kottur in 2022. CtrlS plans a 40-acre park at Chandanvelly with 600 MW or more of potential and 250 MW of sanctioned power for phase one.

Bharat Future City, the planned new town south-east of the airport, is the next frontier. Cushman & Wakefield reports that AWS has started a greenfield campus there, expected live in 2028, and ThePrint reported allotments of 202 acres in Bharat Future City and 98 acres in Chandanvelly to Amazon.

sections.heading: Power in Telangana

blocks.text: Crisil estimates that by FY2030 data centre capacity in Hyderabad could equal about 20% of the city’s current peak power demand, a third of the share it projects for Mumbai. CtrlS reports 250 MW of sanctioned power for the first phase of its Chandanvelly park, an example of the document a buyer should ask to see.

Telangana’s supply rules put contracted demand above 20,000 kVA at 132 kV or above, through a dedicated feeder or a loop-in loop-out arrangement decided by TS Transco, and the consumer pays the full cost of a dedicated service line. HT industrial supply at 132 kV and above was Rs 6.65 per kVAh with a Rs 500 per kVA monthly demand charge in the FY 2024-25 order; TGERC reportedly kept rates unchanged for 2026-27.

The Telangana Data Centres Policy 2016 is the latest dedicated policy we found (Cushman & Wakefield, H1 2025). Large projects in 2025 and 2026 have been handled through project-specific packages; Amazon’s allotments came with reported incentives of Rs 125 crore.

sections.heading: Site risks in Hyderabad

items: Seismic: Hyderabad is Zone II (zone factor 0.10), the lowest of the major data centre cities.
Flood: in October 2020 Ghatkesar recorded 324 mm of rain; 33 people died in the city and losses were estimated at about Rs 9,000 crore. Low-lying plots near lakes and the Musi need a drainage check.
Groundwater: Telangana is among the states where over-exploited assessment units cluster, per the 2025 national assessment. Check the specific unit before relying on borewells.
Airport: Rajiv Gandhi International Airport at Shamshabad sits beside the southern corridor; height NOCs apply within 20 km, or 56 km for instrument airports.

blocks.text: Invariant checks the evidence behind a site’s power (the DISCOM or transmission connection, the open access route, the nearest substations and what else is queued on them), screens seismic zone, flood history, groundwater status and airport height limits, and lists the central and state approvals the project needs with the authority behind each one. In Hyderabad the questions are which 220 kV or 400 kV substation serves the corridor, what is already allocated on it, and the height surface over the plot.

title: Data centres in Noida and Delhi NCR (2026): Noida, Greater Noida, YEIDA and Gurugram
description: Delhi NCR had 183 MW of operational data centre capacity in H1 2026, 156 MW of it in Noida. The UP Data Centre Policy 2026, the YEIDA data centre park and Noida airport height limits shape new sites.
intro: Delhi NCR is India’s third data centre market by Cushman & Wakefield’s count: 183 MW operational in H1 2026, about 10% of the top seven cities, with 360 MW planned. Noida carries almost all of it, 156 MW in 12 facilities, while Gurugram has 18 MW. New campuses are going to Greater Noida and the Yamuna Expressway, where YEIDA has a 100-acre data centre park in Sector 28. The Uttar Pradesh Data Centre Policy 2026, notified on 9 July 2026, sets the incentives, and Noida International Airport, open since June 2026, sets height limits within 20 km.
takeaways: Delhi NCR had 183 MW operational, 27 MW under construction and 360 MW planned in H1 2026; Noida had 156 MW and 1,247 MW at early stage (Cushman & Wakefield).

UP Data Centre Policy 2026 (G.O. 536/78-2-2026, 9 July 2026): base FAR 3.0 plus 1.0 chargeable, 25% land subsidy in western UP including Noida, 100% stamp duty exemption on land from government authorities.
Delhi is Seismic Zone IV, a higher design load than Mumbai or Chennai.
Noida International Airport began commercial flights on 15 June 2026; AAI requires height clearance for construction within 20 km.

blocks.text: Anarock counts 179 MW IT across 18 facilities and forecasts 550 MW by 2030.

sections.heading: Sub-markets: Noida Expressway, Greater Noida, YEIDA and Gurugram

blocks.text: Anarock maps four zones: the Noida Expressway sectors (62, 132, 142, 143 and 150 to 167), Greater Noida around Knowledge Park and Pari Chowk, the Yamuna Expressway towards Jewar under YEIDA, and Gurugram-Manesar on the Haryana side. Campuses include Yotta’s Greater Noida D1 (30 MW live) and D2, NTT in Sector 142, STT GDC in Sector 143, Sify Noida-2 in Sector 132 and AdaniConneX in Sector 62.

YEIDA lists a 100-acre Data Centre Park in Sector 28, next to its medical devices park. Plots under 4,000 sq m are allotted by draw and larger plots by interview, through the Nivesh Mitra portal. AdaniConneX lists 150 MW of potential in Noida, and AM Green signed an MoU with Uttar Pradesh for a 1 GW AI data centre in Greater Noida, with first capacity targeted for 2028.

sections.heading: The UP Data Centre Policy 2026

blocks.text: Uttar Pradesh notified its Data Centre Policy 2026 by G.O. 536/78-2-2026 dated 9 July 2026, repealing the 2021 policy. Parks are 40 MW or more; units are above 2 MW and below 40 MW. Parks get interest subsidy up to Rs 50 crore and a dual-grid subsidy; units get capital subsidy up to Rs 20 crore.

items: Land subsidy of 25% of sector rates in Madhyanchal and Paschimanchal, which include Noida and YEIDA, on land from state agencies.
100% stamp duty exemption on purchase or lease from a government authority, against a bank guarantee released at commercial operation.
Base FAR 3.0 free plus 1.0 chargeable; DG set space, basement storage and rooftop chillers sit outside FAR; ground coverage up to 60%.
100% electricity duty exemption for 10 years and up to 100% transmission and wheeling exemption depending on the renewable source.
Data centres are notified as essential services, and the state assesses water availability before allotting land.

blocks.text: Gurugram and Manesar fall under Haryana, which has its own data centre policy. Compare both states’ terms for an NCR search; the right answer depends on load size and the power route.

sections.heading: Power and water in NCR

blocks.text: Under the UP Supply Code, loads above 10,000 kVA are supplied at 132 kV or 220 kV, and an independent feeder depends on bay and corridor availability at the substation. UPERC’s FY 2026-27 order prices HV-2 large and heavy power, which covers IT and ITeS units notified by the state, at Rs 6.10 per kVAh above 132 kV and Rs 6.40 between 66 and 132 kV in urban areas, plus Rs 270 per kVA per month.

The UP policy supports dual-grid supply for parks and waives transmission and wheeling charges by up to 100%, depending on the renewable source, which matters for green open access contracts. Ask for the specific substation and the DISCOM’s sanction letter; sector-level claims of available power do not tell you what is left for a new load.

Groundwater is the harder constraint. The 2025 national assessment shows over-exploited units clustering in north-west India, and CGWA guidelines bar new industrial abstraction in over-exploited units. SBI lists Gurugram among the water-stressed data centre metros. Plan for treated wastewater or air and closed-loop cooling.

sections.heading: Site risks in Noida and NCR

items: Seismic: Delhi is Zone IV (zone factor 0.24) under the IS 1893 (Part 1) town list (2002 edition, zones retained in 2016), a higher design load than Mumbai, Chennai or Hyderabad. Confirm the zone for the specific YEIDA sector.
Airport: Noida International Airport at Jewar began commercial flights on 15 June 2026. In July 2025 AAI advised that no construction proceed within 20 km without height clearance.
Heat: NCR summers set a high cooling design point, which affects PUE and water use.

blocks.text: Invariant checks the evidence behind a site’s power (the DISCOM or transmission connection, the open access route, the nearest substations and what else is queued on them), screens seismic zone, flood history, groundwater status and airport height limits, and lists the central and state approvals the project needs with the authority behind each one. In NCR the groundwater unit and the Jewar height surface are checked alongside the power route.

title: Data centres in Bengaluru (2026): capacity, Whitefield, Hoskote and the water question
description: Bengaluru had 162 MW of operational data centre capacity in H1 2026, mostly in Whitefield, with 28% vacancy. Karnataka’s 2026-31 policy plans parks at Hoskote, Mysuru and Mangaluru; groundwater is the binding issue.
intro: Bengaluru is a mid-sized data centre market with a large technology economy around it. Cushman & Wakefield counted 162 MW operational in H1 2026, about 9% of the top seven cities, with only 8 MW under construction and 28% colocation vacancy. Most capacity is in Whitefield in the east. Karnataka’s Sustainable Data Centre Policy 2026-31, approved by the Cabinet in September 2026, targets 1 GW by 2031 and pays for low PUE and water efficiency. Water is the constraint: most of the city’s data centres sit in its most water-stressed areas.
takeaways: Bengaluru had 162 MW operational, 8 MW under construction and 92 MW planned in H1 2026 (Cushman & Wakefield). Anarock counts 137 MW IT.
Peripheral East (Whitefield) holds 128 MW; Electronic City 22 MW. Devanahalli in the north is the hyperscale growth corridor.
Karnataka’s 2026-31 policy pays up to Rs 20 crore for PUE between 1.00 and 1.20 and plans parks at Hoskote, Mysuru and Mangaluru.
All Bengaluru Urban groundwater assessment units are reported as over-exploited.
