sections.heading: Sub-markets: Whitefield, Electronic City, Devanahalli and Hoskote

blocks.text: Whitefield and the eastern periphery hold most live capacity. Electronic City in the south hosts NTT Bengaluru 4, about 67 MW IT. Anarock names Devanahalli and North Bengaluru, near the airport, as the hyperscale growth corridor.

Karnataka plans a 500 MW data centre park near Hoskote by 2031, with solar power and treated water committed, and 500 MW across Mysuru and Mangaluru. The 2026-31 policy offers park land on 30 plus 30 year leases with dual-grid power.

sections.heading: Karnataka’s Sustainable Data Centre Policy 2026-31

items: Outlay of Rs 1,300.45 crore and a target of 1 GW by 2031.
PUE incentive up to Rs 20 crore for PUE between 1.00 and 1.20 sustained for three years.
WUE reimbursement up to Rs 30 lakh a year for two years at 0.7 to 1.3 litres per kWh, and treated water reimbursement up to Rs 8 lakh a year for five years.
Custom packages above Rs 3,000 crore, including cable landing stations and desalination.

blocks.text: The earlier Karnataka Data Centre Policy 2022-27 favoured locations outside Bengaluru Urban with capital and land subsidies. Check which policy a project falls under and whether the 2026-31 policy has been formally notified before relying on its terms.

sections.heading: Water: the binding constraint

blocks.text: Newslaundry reported in April 2026 that most of Bengaluru’s data centres are in its most water-stressed eastern and south-eastern areas, with reliance on groundwater. CGWB-based reporting says all Bengaluru Urban assessment units are over-exploited.

Under CGWA guidelines, new industries cannot get groundwater NOCs in over-exploited units, and expansion that increases abstraction is not allowed. A cooling-tower data centre uses about 25.5 million litres per MW per year by Anarock’s estimate, so a new Bengaluru site needs treated water, air-cooled or closed-loop systems from day one.

sections.heading: Other site risks in Bengaluru

items: Seismic: Bengaluru is Zone II (zone factor 0.10) under the IS 1893 (Part 1) town list (2002 edition, zones retained in 2016).
Flood: lake-bed and drain-adjacent plots need a drainage check; several tech corridors sit near the city’s lake chains.
Airport: Kempegowda International Airport at Devanahalli places height surfaces over the northern corridor.

description: Pune had 133 MW of operational data centre capacity in H1 2026 (Cushman & Wakefield), concentrated in Pimpri-Chinchwad and Hinjewadi, with Microsoft’s Central India region and Maharashtra’s data centre incentives.
intro: Pune is Maharashtra’s second data centre market and an overflow for Mumbai. sections.heading: Sub-markets: Pimpri-Chinchwad, Hinjewadi, Chakan and Talegaon

blocks.text: The Pimpri-Chinchwad belt north of the city holds 92 MW in two large facilities. Hinjewadi, the IT park to the west, holds 37 MW across five smaller facilities. AdaniConneX lists 250 MW of potential in Pune, with phase one live from October 2025.
Chakan and Talegaon, the industrial corridors on the Mumbai-Pune axis, have only small planned data centre projects in public so far; treat them as early-stage.

sections.heading: Power and policy in Pune

blocks.text: Maharashtra’s IT/ITES Policy 2023 gives registered data centres a permanent electricity duty exemption, 100% stamp duty exemption on land, and a Rs 1 per unit tariff subsidy for 5 years outside Zone I. Since 9 June 2026 the Integrated Green Data Centre Parks policy covers 20 parks statewide, with a 51% green power requirement and Rs 1 per unit for 10 or 20 years depending on investment.

The same MERC Supply Code applies as in Mumbai: 33 kV up to 10,000 kVA of contract demand (20,000 kVA on an express feeder), extra high voltage above that, and a one-year standard where a new distribution substation is needed. MERC classifies data centres as HT industrial consumers.

Pune’s appeal is partly that it sits outside the Navi Mumbai grid allocation that Structure Research describes as close to committed. Confirm the serving substation and sanction for the specific plot.

sections.heading: Site risks in Pune

items: Seismic: Pune is Zone III (zone factor 0.16) under the IS 1893 (Part 1) town list (2002 edition, zones retained in 2016).
Airport: height clearance under GSR 751(E) covers sites within 20 km of the aerodrome reference point, or 56 km for instrument airports.
Water: check the groundwater assessment unit and the municipal or MIDC supply before planning evaporative cooling.

blocks.text: Invariant checks the evidence behind a site’s power (the DISCOM or transmission connection, the open access route, the nearest substations and what else is queued on them), screens seismic zone, flood history, groundwater status and airport height limits, and lists the central and state approvals the project needs with the authority behind each one. For a Pune site, the comparison with a Navi Mumbai plot is usually about power date and latency, and we lay both out.

title: Data centres in Visakhapatnam (2026): Google’s AI hub, gigawatt campuses, cables and the risks
description: Visakhapatnam has more than 4 GW of announced data centre capacity, led by Google’s US$15 billion AI hub. The checks are power relative to the city’s demand, cyclone exposure, water and new cable landings.
intro: Visakhapatnam has gone from no data centre market to more than 4 GW of announced or early-stage campuses in about a year. Google committed about US$15 billion over 2026 to 2030 for its first India AI hub here, with AdaniConneX and Airtel, and broke ground at Tarluvada on 28 April 2026. Digital Connexion, Colt DCS with RMZ, and AirTrunk have announced campuses of 1 GW or more. Cushman & Wakefield maps more than 4 GW at early or announced stage. Crisil estimates Vizag’s data centre capacity could equal about 80% of the city’s current peak power demand by FY2030.
takeaways: Announced: Google (about US$15 billion, about 1 GW), Digital Connexion (US$11 billion, 1 GW), Colt DCS and RMZ (1.25 GW, Rs 1.77 lakh crore), AirTrunk (up to 1.8 GW in Anakapalli, proposed).
Andhra Pradesh Data Center Policy 4.0 (2024-29) uses project-specific packages for large projects; four projects totalling 3,498 MW were cleared in August 2026.
Cyclone Hudhud crossed the coast over Visakhapatnam on 12 October 2014 with winds of about 180 km/h and a 1.4 m surge.
New subsea routes: Google’s America-India Connect and Sify’s open cable landing station at Rushikonda.

Cleared by SIPC in July 2026, SIPB approval pending; five phases 2027 to 2036
Up to 1.8 GW; about US$11 billion
Plans submitted November 2026, subject to approval
50 MW AI edge data centre and open cable landing station

blocks.text: Andhra Pradesh also cleared four projects totalling 3,498 MW in August 2026 under Policy 4.0, including ReNew’s 1,000 MW in Anakapalli and AM AI Factory’s 512 MW at Amanam. Reported incentives for Google’s subsidiary Raiden Infotech total about Rs 22,000 crore against Rs 87,520 crore of investment, including a 25% discount on about 480 acres.

sections.heading: Power: the scale problem

blocks.text: Crisil’s estimate that data centres could equal about 80% of Visakhapatnam’s current peak demand by FY2030 is the central fact for any site here. Gigawatt campuses need new transmission capacity, and each announced project competes for the same build-out. A site in Vizag needs evidence of which transmission scheme serves it and when, not only a state MoU.
Andhra Pradesh issues incentives for large projects project by project through government orders. Read the project order; the policy text alone does not tell you what a given site gets.

sections.heading: Disadvantages and risks of a data centre in Vizag

items: Cyclone: Hudhud crossed the coast over Visakhapatnam on 12 October 2014 with maximum sustained winds of about 180 km/h, central pressure of 950 hPa and a 1.4 m storm surge at the tide gauge. Design for wind loads and plan for grid outages after landfall.
Coastal rules: sites near the shore fall under the Coastal Regulation Zone Notification 2019, with no-development setbacks from the high tide line.
Water: Andhra Pradesh is among the states with clusters of over-exploited groundwater units in the 2025 national assessment. Large evaporative cooling loads need a non-groundwater source.
Market depth: Vizag has little operating colocation today, so early tenants depend on the hyperscale anchors.
Seismic: Visakhapatnam is Zone II (zone factor 0.10), a low design load.

blocks.text: Invariant checks the evidence behind a site’s power (the DISCOM or transmission connection, the open access route, the nearest substations and what else is queued on them), screens seismic zone, flood history, groundwater status and airport height limits, and lists the central and state approvals the project needs with the authority behind each one. In Vizag the questions are which transmission scheme and substation serve the plot, the cyclone design basis, and the water source.

sections.heading: Cable landings on the east coast

blocks.text: Google’s America-India Connect, announced on 19 February 2026, includes routes from Visakhapatnam and Chennai to South Africa and from Visakhapatnam to Malaysia. Airtel is building a new landing station in Vizag, Sify is building an open landing station at Rushikonda, and Meta’s Waterworth cable is expected to land at Sify’s station.

title: Data centres in Gujarat (2026): Jamnagar, GIFT City, Ahmedabad and Dholera
description: Gujarat’s data centre market is led by Reliance’s AI campus at Jamnagar, where Meta is leasing 168 MW, plus GIFT City and a planned 250 MW Dholera campus. The 2026-29 state policy targets 7.5 GW.
intro: Gujarat is a new data centre state built around a few very large projects rather than a colocation cluster. Reliance is building a multi-gigawatt AI data centre at Jamnagar, said in February 2026 to have more than 120 MW expected online in the second half of 2026; Meta agreed in June 2026 to lease 168 MW there. GIFT City hosts Yotta’s 1 MW G1 facility, and L&T Vyoma signed an MoU for a 250 MW green AI data centre at Dholera. The Viksit Gujarat Data Centre Policy 2026-29, launched on 9 July 2026, targets 7.5 GW and only supports projects of 150 MW or more.
takeaways: Jamnagar: Reliance AI campus; Meta 168 MW lease (June 2026); Google Cloud dedicated AI region announced (August 2025). Estimates of the campus range from 1 GW (Cushman & Wakefield map) to 3 GW (Anarock).

Gujarat’s 2026-29 policy requires at least 150 MW of approved IT load and 51% renewable power, and, according to Cyril Amarchand Mangaldas, makes data centre operations an essential service under the Gujarat ESMA 1972.
GIFT City: Yotta G1, 1 MW live. The 2023-24 Budget proposed data embassies in GIFT IFSC; we found no final notification.
Dholera: L&T Vyoma MoU for 250 MW, Rs 25,000 crore, operations from 2028 subject to feasibility.

sections.heading: Jamnagar: Reliance’s AI campus

blocks.text: Reliance announced a Rs 10 trillion (about US$110 billion) AI compute plan over seven years on 19 February 2026 and said construction of a multi-gigawatt AI data centre at Jamnagar was under way, with more than 120 MW expected online in the second half of 2026, backed by 10 GW of surplus solar. Google Cloud and Reliance announced a dedicated AI cloud region at Jamnagar in August 2025.
Meta signed its first Indian AI data centre deal with Reliance on 10 June 2026: a 168 MW lease at Jamnagar, expected ready within about two years and cooled with desalinated seawater.

sections.heading: GIFT City, Ahmedabad and Dholera

blocks.text: GIFT City, the international financial services centre near Gandhinagar, hosts Yotta’s G1 facility at 1 MW. The Union Budget 2023-24 proposed facilitating data embassies in GIFT IFSC for countries seeking digital continuity; we found no final notification or bilateral agreement as of 2026.

At the India AI Impact Summit in February 2026, Gujarat signed an MoU with L&T Vyoma for a 250 MW green AI data centre at the Dholera Special Investment Region, about Rs 25,000 crore, with operations from 2028 subject to feasibility. The state policy names GIFT City and Dholera as hubs.

sections.heading: The Viksit Gujarat Data Centre Policy 2026-29

items: Eligible projects need at least 150 MW of approved IT load and at least 51% renewable power.
Power tariff subsidy of Rs 1 per unit for 20 years; electricity duty reimbursement of 100% for 20 years; stamp duty and registration 100%.
Interest subsidy up to 4% for 10 years; capital subsidy of 2.5% of eligible fixed capital investment at Dholera; total support capped at 75% of eligible investment.

Open access allowed and dual feeders facilitated; data centre operations treated as an essential service under the Gujarat Essential Services Maintenance Act, 1972, according to Cyril Amarchand Mangaldas.
In force for three years from notification or until 7.5 GW is reached.

blocks.text: The 150 MW floor means the policy targets hyperscale and AI campuses. Smaller facilities fall back on general industrial and IT incentives.

sections.heading: Site risks in Gujarat

items: Seismic: Ahmedabad is Zone III under the IS 1893 (Part 1) town list (2002 edition, zones retained in 2016). Parts of Kutch are high-hazard; check the zone for the specific site. The 2025 seismic map revision was withdrawn in March 2026.

Water: north-west and western India hold a large share of over-exploited groundwater units. Jamnagar’s use of desalinated seawater shows the likely route for large loads, and the state policy supports desalination.
Coast: sites near the shore fall under the Coastal Regulation Zone Notification 2019.

blocks.text: Invariant checks the evidence behind a site’s power (the DISCOM or transmission connection, the open access route, the nearest substations and what else is queued on them), screens seismic zone, flood history, groundwater status and airport height limits, and lists the central and state approvals the project needs with the authority behind each one. In Gujarat, the 150 MW policy floor and the water source are usually settled before the power route.

title: Data centres in Kolkata and East India (2026): New Town, Salt Lake, Bhubaneswar and policy
description: Kolkata had 22 MW of operational data centre capacity in H1 2026, mostly in New Town. West Bengal’s 2021 policy classed data centres as essential services; its term ended around September 2026.
intro: Kolkata is the largest data centre market in East India and one of the smallest of the top seven. Cushman & Wakefield counted 22 MW operational in H1 2026 across six facilities, 18 MW in New Town and 4 MW in Salt Lake, with 13 MW under construction and 71 MW planned. Demand comes from government and smaller enterprises. West Bengal’s Data Centre Policy 2021 classed data centre organisations as essential services and treated their power as industrial; its five-year term ended around September 2026 and the state has said a new policy is coming. Odisha’s 2022 policy is the other incentive regime in the region.
takeaways: Kolkata had 22 MW operational, 13 MW under construction and 71 MW planned in H1 2026, with 19.4% vacancy (Cushman & Wakefield).
New Town holds 18 MW and Salt Lake 4 MW. NTT has inaugurated a 40 MW facility in the city.
West Bengal Data Centre Policy 2021 (notified 6 September 2021): essential services classification, 100% stamp duty exemption, 5-year electricity duty waiver, FAR 3.0 plus 1.0 purchasable.
The government lists West Bengal, Andhra Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh and Chhattisgarh as emerging data centre states.

blocks.text: Cushman & Wakefield attributes Kolkata’s demand to government and small and medium enterprises. Status reports on the Tajpur and Digha landing stations conflict, so treat east-coast cable capacity from Bengal as future rather than current.

sections.heading: Sub-markets and operators

blocks.text: New Town (Rajarhat) holds most of the city’s capacity, with Salt Lake Sector V the older IT district. NTT has inaugurated a 40 MW facility in Kolkata. The government told the Rajya Sabha in August 2026 that West Bengal is one of four emerging data centre states.

sections.heading: West Bengal Data Centre Policy 2021 and what follows

items: Notification No. 490-Estt/ITE-18011/2/2021 dated 6 September 2021, operative for five years or until replaced.
100% stamp duty and registration fee exemption; electricity duty waiver for five years from commercial operation; data centre power treated as industrial.
Dual power grid networks; FAR of 3.0 plus 1.0 purchasable and up to 60% ground coverage; self-certification under notified Acts.
Clause 5.3: data centre organisations classified as essential services.

blocks.text: The five-year term ended around September 2026. In May 2026 the state’s new leadership said a new data centre policy was being prepared. Until it is notified, check with the IT and Electronics Department and Webel which terms apply to a new project.

sections.heading: East India beyond Kolkata: Odisha and Bhubaneswar

blocks.text: Odisha’s State Data Centre Policy 2022, run by OCAC, offers a capital subsidy of 20% of fixed capital investment (excluding land) up to Rs 25 crore per unit, stamp duty exemption, electricity duty and inspection fee exemption for 10 years up to 5 MVA, a 30% power bill subsidy for 5 years up to Rs 2 crore, net SGST reimbursement for 7 years, and reimbursement of transmission and wheeling charges on captive renewable power. Yotta lists Bhubaneswar as a planned edge location.

sections.heading: Site risks in Kolkata

items: Seismic: Kolkata is Zone III (zone factor 0.16) under the IS 1893 (Part 1) town list (2002 edition, zones retained in 2016).
Cyclone and flood: the Bay of Bengal coast is cyclone-exposed, and low-lying plots need a drainage and elevation check.
Airport: Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose International Airport is close to New Town; height NOCs apply within 20 km, or 56 km for instrument airports.

blocks.text: Invariant checks the evidence behind a site’s power (the DISCOM or transmission connection, the open access route, the nearest substations and what else is queued on them), screens seismic zone, flood history, groundwater status and airport height limits, and lists the central and state approvals the project needs with the authority behind each one. In Kolkata the policy status and the substation serving New Town are the first two checks.

title: Data centre companies in India (2026): the largest operators, their capacity and recent deals
description: The largest data centre companies in India by colocation share are NTT, Sify, STT GDC, Nxtra and CtrlS (Anarock, H1 2026), with Yotta, AdaniConneX and new entrants such as AirTrunk, TCS HyperVault and CoreWeave.
intro: India’s data centre market is led by five operators. Anarock’s H1 2026 share table puts NTT at 21%, Sify and STT GDC at 19% each, and Nxtra (Airtel) and CtrlS at 15% each, followed by Yotta at 5%. Behind them sit AdaniConneX, Princeton Digital, Iron Mountain, Equinix, Digital Edge and CapitaLand, plus hyperscalers building their own campuses. In 2026 the capital came in fast: Nxtra raised US$1 billion, CPP Investments committed up to Rs 7,000 crore to CtrlS, AirTrunk bought Lumina CloudInfra, and CoreWeave agreed to take 240 MW from AdaniConneX.
takeaways: Anarock H1 2026 shares: NTT 21%, Sify 19%, STT GDC 19%, Nxtra 15%, CtrlS 15%, Yotta 5%, Princeton Digital 3%, Iron Mountain (Web Werks) 2%, AdaniConneX 1%. Anarock does not state the base; it appears to be third-party colocation capacity.
Company-stated capacity is not comparable across operators: some report built IT load, some operational capacity, some capacity “in operation and development”.
Hyperscalers (AWS, Microsoft, Google) build their own campuses and are not in the colocation share table.
New entrants since 2025: AirTrunk (Lumina), TCS HyperVault, Digital Connexion, Colt DCS with RMZ, CoreWeave as a tenant.

sections.heading: New entrants and global operators

items: Equinix opened MB3 in Mumbai in April 2026 with over US$95 million of initial investment and has committed over US$365 million across Mumbai and Chennai.
Digital Edge is building a planned 400 MW campus in Navi Mumbai with NIIF and Stonepeak; BOM2 (48.4 MW) topped out in August 2026, fully committed.
CapitaLand is building a 53 MW gross facility in Ambattur, Chennai, due by the end of 2026.
AirTrunk, owned by Blackstone, acquired Lumina CloudInfra in April 2026, with about 600 MW planned across Mumbai, Chennai and Hyderabad.
Colt DCS and RMZ formed a US$1.7 billion joint venture in November 2024 for Navi Mumbai and Chennai.
TCS HyperVault, with up to Rs 18,000 crore including TPG, targets 1 GW or more; OpenAI is its first customer at 100 MW.
Digital Connexion, the Reliance, Brookfield and Digital Realty joint venture, runs a 100 MW Chennai campus and plans 1 GW in Visakhapatnam.

sections.heading: Hyperscalers building their own data centres

blocks.text: AWS, Microsoft and Google run or are building their own campuses. AWS operates regions in Mumbai and Hyderabad, Microsoft runs four Indian regions including India South Central in Hyderabad, and Google is building its AI hub in Visakhapatnam with AdaniConneX and Airtel. Invest India and Cushman & Wakefield report that hyperscalers took more than 80% of absorption in H1 2026.

For a buyer of capacity, the useful question is not which company is largest but which one has firm power for the MW and date you need. Ask for the DISCOM sanction or connection agreement behind the hall you would occupy.

title: Mumbai vs Chennai vs Hyderabad for data centres (2026): capacity, power, policy, land and risk
description: Mumbai has the scale and cables but a nearly committed grid allocation; Chennai has cables and spare halls but flood risk and a lapsed policy; Hyderabad has the biggest hyperscale pipeline and the lowest seismic zone.
intro: Mumbai, Chennai and Hyderabad are India’s three main choices for a large data centre, and each wins on a different test. Mumbai has about half of top-seven-city live capacity (Cushman & Wakefield), 13 cable landing stations and the lowest vacancy, but Structure Research reports its Navi Mumbai grid allocation is close to committed. Chennai has seven landing stations and the most spare colocation, but carries flood and cyclone risk and its state policy window closed on 31 March 2026. Hyderabad has the second largest pipeline, Microsoft and AWS regions and Seismic Zone II, but no cable landings.
takeaways: Pick Mumbai for interconnection and latency to cables; plan for power evidence to be the hardest part.
Pick Chennai for available halls today and east-coast cables; check flood exposure at plot level.
Pick Hyderabad for hyperscale-scale land and power headroom relative to demand; accept no local cable landing.
Rents are within a narrow band across the three; land and power date differ far more.

title: India vs Singapore vs Johor for data centres (2026): capacity, power, policy, water and cost
description: Singapore rations new capacity through allocation calls, Johor has signed GW-scale power deals but is tightening water, and India offers lower build cost, rents 30 to 35% below peers and a tax holiday to 2047.
intro: India, Singapore and Johor in Malaysia compete for the same Asian cloud and AI capacity, under very different constraints. Singapore had about 1.4 GW across more than 70 data centres in 2024 and now releases new capacity through allocation calls; its second call in December 2025 offered at least 200 MW with a PUE of 1.25 at full load. Malaysia’s utility TNB had signed supply agreements for 59 data centre projects totalling 8.3 GW by mid-2026, while Johor, the main Malaysian cluster, tightened water rules. India had roughly 1.8 GW live in H1 2026, build costs that Cushman & Wakefield puts about 23% below Malaysia, and a tax holiday to 2047 for foreign cloud companies using Indian data centres.
takeaways: Singapore: capacity is allocated, not open. DC-CFA2 (launched 1 December 2025) offered at least 200 MW with PUE 1.25 at full load, Green Mark Platinum and 50% green energy pathways.

Johor: TNB had 59 data centre projects and 8.3 GW under supply agreements by July 2026. Johor set up a committee to vet data centres’ water demand in August 2025 and raised the data centre water tariff.
India: no national cap; state policies compete with incentives. Build cost about US$7.4 million per MW (Cushman & Wakefield), rents 30 to 35% below peer markets (Crisil).
The figures are not like for like: Singapore’s is a 2024 government capacity figure, Malaysia’s is maximum demand under power contracts, India’s is operational capacity from market reports.

sections.heading: Singapore: scarce capacity, strict conditions

blocks.text: Singapore paused new data centres in 2019, ran an 80 MW pilot allocation in 2023, and launched its Green Data Centre Roadmap on 30 May 2024, with at least 300 MW of additional capacity in the near term and more for operators using green energy. The second Data Centre Call for Application opened on 1 December 2025 for at least 200 MW and closed to proposals on 31 March 2026.

Selected applicants must reach PUE of 1.25 or better at full design load, obtain Green Mark for Data Centres 2024 Platinum, and power at least half of the new capacity through eligible green pathways such as biomethane, hydrogen, ammonia or solar. The result is high cost and limited supply, which pushes overflow demand to Johor and, increasingly, India.

sections.heading: Johor: fast power, tightening water

blocks.text: RHB Research, reported by The Star in July 2026, counted TNB electricity supply agreements for 59 data centre projects with a combined 8.3 GW, of which 36 projects with a maximum capacity of 4.5 GW were completed. These are contracted maximum demands, not IT load in use.

Water is Johor’s constraint. The state set up a special technical committee in August 2025 to vet each data centre’s impact on water demand, and a data centre water tariff of RM5.33 per cubic metre took effect on 1 August 2025.

sections.heading: India: lower cost, slower power, state-by-state rules

blocks.text: India’s advantages are cost and domestic demand. Cushman & Wakefield puts construction at about US$7.4 million per MW, about 23% below Malaysia and 26% below Australia, and Crisil reports Indian rents 30 to 35% below peer markets. The Budget 2026-27 tax holiday to 2047 targets exactly the export use case that Singapore and Johor serve today.

The trade-offs are power timelines and fragmentation. There is no national data centre law; each state sets its own incentives, and grid connection runs through state utilities. Structure Research reports Navi Mumbai’s grid allocation for data centres is close to committed, pushing new Mumbai builds to Panvel, Taloja and Rasayani. Beyond Mumbai, Hyderabad holds 18% of upcoming supply and Visakhapatnam more than 4 GW announced or early-stage.

title: AI data centres in India (2026): gigawatt campuses, IndiaAI GPUs and power needs
description: India’s AI data centre build-out is led by gigawatt campuses in Visakhapatnam, Jamnagar and Navi Mumbai, and IndiaAI Mission compute that passed 45,000 GPUs in June 2026 at around Rs 65 per GPU-hour.
intro: AI demand is reshaping India’s data centre market from colocation halls into gigawatt campuses. Google is building an AI hub of about 1 GW in Visakhapatnam, Reliance is building a multi-gigawatt AI campus at Jamnagar where Meta is leasing 168 MW, OpenAI has taken 100 MW from TCS HyperVault with an option to reach 1 GW, and CoreWeave will take 240 MW at AdaniConneX in Navi Mumbai. The government’s IndiaAI Mission had more than 45,000 GPUs in its shared compute pool by June 2026, priced around Rs 65 per GPU-hour. Cushman & Wakefield’s AI scenario puts India at about 8 GW by 2030.
takeaways: Announced gigawatt-scale AI campuses: Google in Visakhapatnam, Reliance at Jamnagar, Digital Connexion and Colt DCS with RMZ in Vizag, AirTrunk in Anakapalli (proposed), TCS HyperVault, AM Green in Greater Noida (MoU).
IndiaAI GPU pool: 18,693 offered (January 2025), 34,333 (May 2025), 38,000+ at Rs 65 per hour (February 2026), 45,000+ (June 2026).
AI racks run 30 to 60 kW against 8 to 10 kW for traditional racks (Anarock). Power per GPU, not floor area, sizes the site.

sections.heading: Power for AI data centres in India

blocks.text: An AI campus is sized by power per GPU. Anarock puts AI racks at 30 to 60 kW against 8 to 10 kW for traditional racks, and SBI notes direct-to-chip and immersion cooling start beyond about 15 kW per rack. A 100 MW AI hall therefore needs a high-voltage grid connection with a firm energisation date, not a distribution feeder.

That is why the gigawatt projects cluster where new transmission can be built: Visakhapatnam, Jamnagar with captive solar, and the outer Mumbai belt. Crisil estimates Vizag’s data centre capacity could equal about 80% of the city’s current peak demand by FY2030.

title: Data centre investment in India (2026): hyperscaler commitments, deals and what to diligence
description: Announced data centre investment in India passed US$180 billion by September 2026, led by Amazon, Microsoft, Google, Reliance and Adani. The commitments are large; the power behind each campus is what to check.
intro: Data centre investment in India has grown faster than the capacity it will build. Invest India and Cushman & Wakefield count disclosed commitments of US$27 billion in 2023, US$29.6 billion in 2024, US$56.4 billion in 2025 and US$184 billion in January to September 2026. Amazon has committed US$48 billion for 2026 to 2030, Microsoft US$17.5 billion for 2026 to 2029, and Google about US$15 billion for its Visakhapatnam AI hub. Reliance announced a US$110 billion AI compute plan and Adani US$100 billion through 2035. The Budget 2026-27 added a tax holiday to 2047 for foreign cloud companies using Indian data centres.
takeaways: Disclosed commitments: US$184 billion in January to September 2026 alone (Invest India and Cushman & Wakefield). CBRE counts Rs 15.29 lakh crore (US$173 billion) cumulative since 2021.
Equity mix of current investments: 61% foreign, 39% domestic.
Long-tenor debt costs about 9.5 to 10.5% for up to 12 years, helped by infrastructure status (Anarock).
A commitment is not capacity. The diligence question is whether the campus has a firm power connection and date.

CBRE counts Rs 3.34 lakh crore (US$38 billion) in H1 2026 and Rs 15.29 lakh crore (US$173 billion) since 2021. Anarock cites more than US$300 billion of commitments.

sections.heading: What to diligence before investing in an Indian data centre

items: Power: the DISCOM sanction letter or transmission connection agreement, the substation and voltage, the energisation date, and what else is queued on the same substation.
Policy: which state policy applies, whether its window is still open (Tamil Nadu’s closed on 31 March 2026), and whether incentives are in a project-specific order.
Site: seismic zone, flood history, groundwater unit status, airport height limits and coastal rules.
Contracts: tenor (Crisil reports 15 to 20 years is now common), tenant concentration and power pass-through.

blocks.text: Infrastructure status for data centres of 5 MW or more of IT load, notified on 11 October 2022, gives access to long-tenor infrastructure lending. Anarock puts long-tenor debt at about 9.5 to 10.5% for up to 12 years.
